Falstaff!: Dr. Caius bursts violently into the Garter Inn, shouting for Falstaff.
Olà!: Falstaff answers with nonchalant composure from his table.
Oh! che vi piglia?: The colloquial idiom 'che vi piglia?' means 'what has come over you?' or 'what is the matter with you?' (literally: 'what seizes you?').
Caius uses the informal second-person singular ('tu') in indignant reproach. Italian determiner syntax 'i miei servi' translates directly as 'my servants'.
Falstaff completely ignores Caius's outrage, demanding more Spanish sherry (sack). Note that 'di' is a preposition.
Hai fiaccata la mia giumenta baia,: You have exhausted my bay mare,
The past participle 'fiaccata' agrees with the feminine direct object 'la mia giumenta baia'. Determiner syntax translates to 'my bay mare'.
Continuation of Caius's accusation: '[Hai] sforzata la mia casa'. Lowercase initial matches verse enjambment.
Falstaff retorts with a bawdy double entendre: he broke into the house, but spared Caius's woman.
Troppa grazia! Una vecchia cisposa. Ampi: Too much favor! An old blear-eyed woman. Portly sir,

Caius sarcastically scoffs at Falstaff's boast of having spared his housekeeper: she is just an old blear-eyed crone anyway ('Troppa grazia!' = 'What a huge favor!'). He then sneers at Falstaff's immense physical girth as 'Ampio messere' (vast/portly sir).
se foste venti volte John Falstaff caval: if you were twenty times Sir John Falstaff,
Caius shifts to the formal 'voi' ('foste') to challenge Falstaff's chivalric title of knight ('cavaliere').
I will compel you to answer me.

v'obbligherò a rispondermi..meaning: I will compel you / oblige you

The clitic pronoun 'v'' (voi) is elided before 'obbligherò' (future 1st person singular).
Falstaff brazenly confesses to every single accusation without hesitation or remorse.
E poi?: Nannetta's prompt question echoing Fenton's words, playfully encouraging him to explain what follows peace.

L'ho fatto apposta..meaning: I did it / I have done it

The clitic 'L'' represents the neuter direct object pronoun 'lo' ('it').
I will appeal to the royal council.
'Real' is an apocope of 'reale'. In Shakespeare's *The Merry Wives of Windsor*, Caius threatens to make a Star Chamber matter of it.

Vatti con dio..meaning: go away (imperative 2nd singular with reflexive pronoun)

'Vatti con dio' is a formula of dismissal meaning 'Be on your way and leave me in peace'.
Sta' zitto o avrai le beffe; quest'è il: Hold your tongue or you will be mocked; this is my counsel.

Caius threatened to appeal to the royal council ('consiglio real'), so Falstaff mocks him with his own 'consiglio' (advice): shut up, or you will be laughed out of court and become a laughingstock ('avrai le beffe').
Al diavolo!: A sharp curse of dismissal equivalent to 'Go to the devil!'
Bardolfo!: Caius turns his accusations toward Falstaff's rogue companion Bardolfo.
'Ser' is an archaic Tuscan title of respect prefixed to titles or names (derived from 'messere').
'Ier' is an apocope of 'ieri' (yesterday), frequent in Tuscan and poetic verse.
Bardolfo facetiously feigns hangover agony to elicit Caius's medical sympathy.
I feel sick. Assist me with your diagnosis. My bowel is

Bardolfo feigns terrible hangover sickness and facetiously begs Dr. Caius—who is a physician—for a professional medical prognosis ('pronostico'), hoping to distract Caius from the robbery accusations.
guasto. Malanno agli osti che dan la cal: ruined. A plague upon innkeepers who put lime in the wine!

Corrupt Renaissance innkeepers cut sour or spoiled wine with lime (calcium oxide) to mask acidity and sweeten it; Bardolfo hypocritically blames this adulterated wine for his violent hangover rather than the vast quantities of sherry he consumed.
Vedi questa meteora?: Bardolfo comically points to his famously bulbous, bright red, alcohol-inflamed nose, grandly describing it as a blazing 'meteor' or beacon in the sky.

La vedo..meaning: it (feminine direct object pronoun referring to 'meteora')

The clitic pronoun 'La' refers back to the feminine noun 'meteora' (Bardolfo's nose), requiring English 'it'.
Essa si corca: Bardolfo continues personifying his blazing red nose as a celestial meteor that 'lies down' (sets) every night when he goes to bed. 'Corcarsi' is archaic Tuscan for 'coricarsi' (to lie down / go to bed; of a celestial body, to set).
Syntactic continuation from the previous line ('Essa si corca / rossa così ogni notte').
Pronostico di forca!: Caius delivers his furious diagnosis: rather than medical treatment, Caius diagnoses that Bardolfo's drunken knavery will inevitably lead him to be hanged from the gallows ('forca').
M'hai fatto ber, furfante, con lui, narr: You made me drink, scoundrel, with him, telling tall tales;

Caius accuses Bardolfo of plying him with wine while distracting him with 'frasche' (literally branches/twigs, an Italian idiom for tall tales, frivolous gossip, and nonsense) so they could pick his pockets.
poi, quando fui ben ciùschero, m'hai vuo: then, when I was completely tipsy, you emptied my pockets.
'Ciùschero' is a Tuscan colloquial term meaning pleasantly tipsy or intoxicated. Caius complains that once he was thoroughly drunk, Bardolfo cleaned out his pockets.
Pistola!: Falstaff summons his other follower, Pistol (Pistola).
Hai tu vuotate: The past participle 'vuotate' agrees in gender and number with the direct object 'le tasche' in the next line.
le tasche a quel messere?: Continuation from previous line: 'Hai tu vuotate / le tasche a quel messere?'
Come s'atteggia al niego quel ceffo da b: How that liar's mug strikes an attitude of denial!
'Niego' is an archaic Tuscan literary variant of 'diniego' (denial). 'Ceffo' is a derogatory term for a brute or villain's snout/face.
Qui c'eran due scellini del regno d'Edoa: Here there were two shillings from the reign of Edward
Refers to English King Edward VI shillings ('two Edward shovel-boards' in Shakespeare's *Merry Wives of Windsor*).
A 'mezzacorona' (half-crown) was an English coin valued at two shillings and sixpence.
Not a trace of them remains.
'Ne' is the partitive clitic referring to the coins; 'riman' is an apocope of 'rimane'.
Padron, chiedo di battermi con quest'arm: Master, I ask to fight with this wooden weapon.
Pistola grandiosely demands formal chivalric permission from Falstaff to duel Dr. Caius, waving a wooden tavern slat or bill as his 'weapon of wood' with mock-heroic swagger.

Vi smentisco!.meaning: I deny / give the lie to / contradict

Vi smentisco!: In chivalric duel codes, 'smentire' ('giving the lie') was a grave formal provocation that demanded immediate combat; Pistola affects aristocratic dueling etiquette despite being a penniless tavern rogue.
Bifolco! tu parli a un gentiluomo!: Churl! you speak to a gentleman!
Dr. Caius is outraged that a vulgar ruffian dares challenge him to a duel, calling Pistola a 'bifolco' (a base peasant/ox-plowman) who has no right to address a gentleman of standing.
Gonzo!: Tuscan insult for a gullible, foolish dupe.
Pezzente!: Caius mocks Pistola's threadbare, penniless condition.
Can!: 'Can' is an apocope of 'cane', an epithet denoting utter baseness.
Spauracchio!: Derides Pistola's gaunt, ragged, menacing appearance.
Gnomo!: Pistola mocks Caius's short stature or odd appearance.
Germoglio di mandragora!: Caius calls Pistola a 'sprout of mandrake'—a poisonous mythical plant whose bifurcated roots were said to resemble a deformed little human and shriek like demons when uprooted—insulting Pistola's grotesque appearance and depravity.
Chi?: Falstaff is startled by the unexpected suspicion of infidelity, blurting out a quick interrogative.
Dr. Caius fires back instantly, pointing the finger right back at Ford.
Caius insists that Ford is the primary dupe who engineered the whole debacle.
Saette!: 'Saette!' (literally arrows/lightning bolts) is an oath of fury akin to 'Zounds!' or 'Thunder and lightning!'.

Non scaricarti qui!.meaning: to discharge oneself / go off / vent (reflexive infinitive with clitic ti)

Non scaricarti qui!: Falstaff makes a witty pun on Pistola's name ('Pistol'): he commands his hot-headed henchman (a firearm) not to 'discharge' (scaricarsi / fire / explode with rage) inside the inn.
Bardolfo! Chi ha vuotato le tasche a que: Bardolfo! Who emptied that gentleman's pockets?
It was one of the two.
Costui beve, poi pe 'l gran bere: This fellow drinks, then from the heavy drinking

Costui beve, poi pe 'l gran bere.meaning: this fellow / this man (pejorative demonstrative pronoun)
for the / through the (archaic contraction of per + il)

Costui beve, poi pe 'l gran bere: Bardolfo concocts a brazen excuse: he claims Dr. Caius simply drank excessively ('pe 'l gran bere'), using the pejorative demonstrative 'Costui' ('this fellow'). 'Pe 'l' is an archaic contraction of 'per il'.
perde i suoi cinque sensi, poi ti narra: loses his five senses, then tells you a fairy tale
Bardolfo argues that Caius lost all his senses through drink and fabricated the whole robbery as a drunken hallucination ('favola' = fairy tale/fiction). 'Ti' is an ethical dative.
ch'egli ha sognato mentre dormì sotto la: that he dreamed while he slept under the table.

ch'egli ha sognato mentre dormì sotto la.meaning: that he (contraction of conjunction che + pronoun egli)

ch'egli ha sognato mentre dormì sotto la: Bardolfo claims Caius passed out dead drunk under the tavern table and dreamed the entire theft while asleep.
L'odi? Se ti capaciti, del ver tu sei si: Do you hear him? If you see reason, you are sure of the truth.

L'odi? Se ti capaciti, del ver tu sei si.meaning: do you hear him (clitic lo + odi)
you convince yourself / come to terms

L'odi? Se ti capaciti, del ver tu sei si: 'Capacitarsi' means to understand or convince oneself of a fact. 'Ver' is an apocope of 'vero'.
The facts are denied. Go in peace.
Falstaff parodies legal court formulas ('I fatti son negati') coupled with mock priestly benediction ('Vattene in pace').
Giuro: Caius begins his solemn resolution, continuing across lines 72 and 73.
che se mai mi ubriaco ancora all'osteria: that if ever I get drunk again at the tavern
Dr. Caius makes the solemn vow directly adapted from Shakespeare's *Merry Wives of Windsor*.
sarà fra gente onesta, sobria, civile e: it will be among honest, sober, civil, and pious people.
Caius's famous vow: to only get drunk 'in honest, civil, godly company'.
Bardolfo and Pistola mockingly chant a solemn liturgical 'Amen'.
Cessi l'antifona. La urlate in contratte: Cease the antiphon. You howl it off the beat.
Falstaff cuts off Bardolfo and Pistola's mock-church choir chanting of 'Amen', rebuking them like an irritable choirmaster for howling it out of time / off the beat ('in contrattempo').
L'arte sta in questa massima: «rubar con: The art lies in this maxim: «to steal with grace and in time».
Falstaff lectures his henchmen on the fine art of thievery: a true master thief must steal with elegance ('garbo') and perfect timing ('a tempo', playing on the musical term for keeping time).
Falstaff ironically treats crime as a fine art and chides his men as unrefined amateurs.
«Sei polli: sei scellini,: Falstaff begins reading the tavern bill line by line.
trenta giarre di Xeres: due lire; tre ta: thirty jars of sherry: two pounds; three turkeys...»
'Giarre' is an archaic spelling of 'giare' (flagons/jars). 'Lire' translates English pounds.
Falstaff orders Bardolfo to search his coin purse to settle the tavern bill.
«Due fagiani, un'acciuga.»: Quotes Prince Hal's reading of Falstaff's tavern bill in Shakespeare's *Henry IV, Part 1* ('an anchovy and sack').
A mark, a mark, a penny.
Bardolfo counts the meager coins remaining in the purse: Falstaff is destitute.
Falstaff orders Bardolfo to rummage through their pockets and tavern purse to find money for the bill. 'Fruga' is the second-person singular imperative of 'frugare' (to search thoroughly).
Bardolfo's dejected reply that he has already searched the purse and found nothing. Passato prossimo of 'frugare' using auxiliary 'avere'.
Fruga!: Falstaff refuses to accept that they are completely broke and furiously repeats the command: 'Search again!'
Here there is not a penny left.
Bardolfo reveals the painful truth that they are totally out of money. 'Spicciolo' denotes small change or copper coins; double negative 'non c'è più' means 'there isn't any more left'.
Sei la mia distruzione!: Falstaff blames Bardolfo for drinking away all his money. Uses the standard Italian possessive structure with definite article 'la mia distruzione' (literally 'the my destruction', meaning 'my ruin').
Spendo ogni sette giorni dieci ghinee! B: I spend ten guineas every seven days! Drunkard!

Falstaff complains about their ruinous tavern tab, adapting Shakespeare's 'I sit at ten pounds a week' (Merry Wives I.3). 'Beone' is an expressive augmentative noun derived from 'bere' (to drink), meaning a heavy sot.
So che se andiam, la notte, di taverna i: I know that if we go, at night, from tavern to tavern,
Falstaff begins his famous teasing about Bardolfo's alcohol-reddened nose (drawn from 1 Henry IV, III.3). 'Andiam' is an apocope of 'andiamo' (we go).
quel tuo naso ardentissimo mi serve da l: that blazing nose of yours serves me as a lantern;

Falstaff jokes that Bardolfo's glowing red nose lights their way in the dark like a street lantern (Shakespeare's 'thou art our admiral, thou bearest the lantern in the poop'). 'Ardentissimo' is the absolute superlative of 'ardente'.
ma quel risparmio d'olio me lo consumi i: but that saving on oil you consume for me in wine.

ma quel risparmio d'olio me lo consumi i.meaning: it on me (ethical dative 'me' + direct object 'lo')

ma quel risparmio d'olio me lo consumi i: The comedic punchline: Falstaff points out that while Bardolfo's glowing red nose saves him money on buying lantern oil at night, Bardolfo drinks away all the savings in wine. 'Me lo consumi' pairs an ethical dative 'me' with direct object 'lo'.
Son trent'anni che abbevero quel fungo p: For thirty years I have watered that purple mushroom!

Falstaff groans that he has paid for Bardolfo's drinking habits for thirty years. 'Fungo porporino' (purple mushroom) is a comic grotesque metaphor for Bardolfo's bulbous, wine-flushed nose (rhinophyma).
Falstaff's blunt financial verdict addressed to Bardolfo: he is simply too expensive to keep around as a dependent.
And you as well. Host! another bottle.
Falstaff turns to his other freeloading follower, Pistola ('And you too'), but despite his complaints about insolvency, immediately orders another bottle of wine from the innkeeper ('Oste!').
Mi struggete le carni! Se Falstaff s'ass: You consume my flesh! If Falstaff grows thin

Mi struggete le carni! Se Falstaff s'ass.meaning: you consume / melt away (2nd person plural)

Mi struggete le carni! Se Falstaff s'ass: Falstaff melodrammatically complains that the stress of keeping his useless men is causing him to lose weight. For Falstaff, growing thin ('s'assottiglia', from 'assottigliarsi') would ruin his grand physical majesty.
non è più lui, nessuno più l'ama; in que: he is no longer himself, no one loves him any more; in this paunch

Falstaff grandly uses illeism (referring to himself in the third person): if he loses his bulk, he won't be Falstaff anymore, and no woman will love him. 'Addome' (paunch/belly) is the core of his pride.
c'è un migliaio di lingue che annunciano: there are a thousand tongues proclaiming my name!
Falstaff personifies his colossal belly as an empire where a thousand voices proclaim his legendary fame. Collective singular 'migliaio' governing the plural relative verb 'annunciano'.
Falstaff immenso!: Pistola flatters his master by exclaiming at his sheer size. An exclamatory apostrophe celebrating Falstaff's colossal girth.
Enorme Falstaff!: Bardolfo joins in the flattering chorus, echoing Pistola with another synonym celebrating Sir John's monumental size.
Falstaff caresses his vast paunch and proudly proclaims it his royal dominion. Elision of 'questo' before 'è' ('Quest'è').
Lo ingrandirò. Ma è tempo d'assottigliar: I will enlarge it. But it is time to sharpen our wits.

Lo ingrandirò. Ma è tempo d'assottigliar.meaning: I will enlarge / expand (1st person singular future)

Lo ingrandirò. Ma è tempo d'assottigliar: Falstaff vows to make his belly even bigger, but since they are broke, he must sharpen his wits to raise cash. Plays cleverly on 'assottigliare' (he refuses to let his body grow thin, but resolves to sharpen his intellect via the idiom 'assottigliar l'ingegno').
PISTOLA E BARDOLFO: Score cue indicating that Falstaff's two ruffian followers, Pistola and Bardolfo, speak in unison.

Assottigliam..meaning: let us sharpen / refine (1st person plural hortative, apocopated)

Pistola and Bardolfo eagerly agree: 'Let us sharpen our wits!' First-person plural hortative subjunctive with apocope from 'assottigliamo', echoing Falstaff's idiom 'assottigliar l'ingegno'.
V'è noto un tal, qui del paese,: Is there known to you a certain fellow, here from the town,

Falstaff begins his scheme to seduce wealthy local townswomen for money, asking if they know a certain burgher. 'V'è noto' elides the dative plural pronoun 'vi' (to you) before 'è' (is known). 'Un tal' is apocopated from 'un tale'.
che ha nome Ford?: Falstaff names the wealthy Windsor citizen Master Ford. The idiom 'avere nome' means 'to be named / to bear the name'.
That man is a wealthy burgher...
Falstaff describes Ford as a prosperous, wealthy burgher. Note the poetic apocopes 'uom' (from 'uomo') and 'gran' (from 'grande').
Pistola chiming in that Ford is wealthier and more lavish than Croesus ('Creso'), the ancient Lydian king famous for boundless gold. 'Liberal' is apocopated from 'liberale' (generous / open-handed).
È un Lord!: Bardolfo exaggerates Ford's lavish wealth by calling him a 'Lord', using the English loanword colloquially in Italian to denote aristocratic fortune.
Falstaff brings the focus to Ford's attractive wife, Alice. Italian possessive adjective 'sua' omits the definite article before the singular kinship noun 'moglie'.
Atto primo Falstaff: Libretto section header marking Act I of Falstaff in the score.
Pistola delivers the crucial detail: Alice holds the keys to Ford's strongbox ('scrigno'). Boito adapts Shakespeare's 'she has all the rule of her husband's purse' (Merry Wives I.3). 'Tien' is apocopated from 'tiene'.
È quella! O amor! Sguardo di stella!: She is the one! O love! Starlike glance!
Falstaff immediately explodes into romantic rhapsody once he realizes Alice holds the money: 'She's the one!'. Note the apocope of 'amore' to 'amor'.
Collo di cigno! e il labbro? Un fior. Un: Swan neck! and her lip? A flower. A flower that smiles.

Falstaff parodies classic Petrarchan love poetry, praising Alice's swan neck and smiling lips. In Italian literary diction, 'un fior che ride' uses 'ridere' in the poetic sense of blossoming or smiling brightly.
Alice è il nome, e un giorno, come passa: Alice is her name, and one day, as she saw me pass
Falstaff narrates his supposed encounter with Alice Ford. Inverted word order 'come passar mi vide' (as she saw me pass) with apocopated infinitive 'passar' and clitic 'mi'.
ne' suoi paraggi, rise. M'ardea l'estro: in her vicinity, she smiled. The amorous frenzy burned in me

Falstaff convinces himself that Alice's polite smile in the street was passionate flirtation, setting off his amorous lust. 'Ne'' is an apocope for 'nei' (in the), and 'ardea' is poetic imperfect for 'ardeva' with dative 'mi'.
nel cor. La dèa vibrava raggi di specchi: in my heart. The goddess beamed rays of a burning mirror,
Falstaff imagines Alice's gaze focusing the sun's rays on him like Archimedes' burning mirror ('specchio ustorio') to set his lust on fire. Apocope of 'cuore' to 'cor'.
su me, su me, sul fianco baldo, sul gran: upon me, upon me, upon my bold flank, upon my great chest,
Falstaff's self-delusion in full glory: he imagines her gazing with burning desire upon his massive body, bold hips, and enormous chest. Features repeated prepositions 'su... sul'.
sul maschio piè, sul fusto saldo, erto,: upon my manly foot, upon my trunk sturdy, erect, capacious;
Falstaff continues extolling his physical attributes: his manly feet and sturdy, upright, roomy ('capace') torso. 'Piè' is truncated from 'piede', and 'fusto' literally means a tree trunk.
e il suo desir in lei fulgea sì al mio c: and her desire in her shone so joined to mine
Falstaff believes her lust matched his so perfectly that it shone forth visibly. 'Desir' is poetic apocope for 'desiderio', and 'fulgea' is archaic imperfect for 'fulgeva' (shone).
che parea dir: «Io son di Sir John Falst: that it seemed to say: 'I belong to Sir John Falstaff.'
Falstaff concludes his fantasy: Alice's gaze seemed to declare 'I belong to Sir John Falstaff!' 'Parea' is poetic imperfect for 'pareva', and 'dir' is apocopated from 'dire'.
Bardolfo cuts through Falstaff's romantic daydream by dryly acting as a scribe, announcing a punctuation full stop ('period').
E a capo. Un'altra; e questa ha nome Mar: And new line. Another one; and this one is named Margaret.
Falstaff doesn't miss a beat and continues his dictation like a merchant: 'New line/paragraph! Another woman!'. He introduces Meg Page (using her Italian name Margherita).
Pistola provides her familiar English nickname 'Meg'. 'Chiaman' is apocopated from 'chiamano'.
She too is infatuated with my charms.
Falstaff boasts that Meg Page too is madly infatuated with his charms. 'Anch'essa' elides 'anche essa' (she too); 'invaghita di' means enamored/infatuated with.
E anch'essa tien le chiavi dello scrigno: And she too holds the keys of the coffer. These women
The punchline of Falstaff's scheme: Meg Page also holds the keys to her husband's strongbox. 'Tien' is apocopated from 'tiene'. The pronoun 'Costoro' (these women) is enjambed into the next line.
saran le mie Golconde e le mie Coste d'o: shall be my Golcondas and my Gold Coasts!

saran le mie Golconde e le mie Coste d'o.meaning: Golcondas (ancient diamond-mining city of India, emblem of wealth)

saran le mie Golconde e le mie Coste d'o: Falstaff envisions the two wealthy wives as his personal treasure houses (adapting Shakespeare's 'they shall be my East and West Indies'). Golconda was an Indian city famed for diamond mines; the Gold Coast was known for gold reserves. 'Saran' is apocopated from 'saranno'.
Guardate. Io sono ancora una piacente es: Look. I am still a pleasing summer
Falstaff shows off his physique to his followers, claiming that despite his age, he is still an attractive, virile man. 'Piacente' is the present participle of 'piacere' used adjectivally.
di san Martino. A voi, due lettere infuo: of Saint Martin. To you, two fiery letters.

'Estate di san Martino' (St. Martin's summer) is the Italian idiom for Indian summer (a warm spell in late autumn, echoing Hal calling Falstaff 'All-hallown summer' in 1 Henry IV). He hands them two passionate love letters.
Tu porta questa a Meg; tentiam la sua vi: You carry this to Meg; let us test her virtue.

Tu porta questa a Meg; tentiam la sua vi.meaning: let us test / tempt (1st person plural hortative, apocopated)

Tu porta questa a Meg; tentiam la sua vi: Falstaff instructs Bardolfo to deliver one letter to Meg Page to test her fidelity. 'Tentiam' is hortative 1st person plural apocopated from 'tentiamo'.
Already I see that your nose burns with zeal.
Falstaff mocks Bardolfo's glowing red nose, joking that it is already blazing with holy zeal to deliver the love letter.
And you carry this to Alice.
Falstaff commands Pistola to deliver the identical second letter to Alice Ford. Note the euphonic 'd' in 'ad Alice'.
I wear a sword at my side.

Porto una spada al fianco..meaning: I wear / carry (1st person singular present)

Pistola proudly refuses, insisting he is a soldier who wears a sword, not a courier of illicit love notes (Shakespeare's Merry Wives I.3: 'Shall I Sir Pandarus of Troy become, and by my side wear steel?').
I am not a Sir Pandarus. I refuse.

Non sono un messer Pandarus. Ricuso..meaning: I refuse / reject (1st person singular present)

Pistola declares he will not act as a pimp (alluding to Pandarus, who procured Cressida for Troilus). 'Ricuso' means 'I refuse'.

Saltimbanco..meaning: to mount a bench (etymological origin of saltimbanco)

Falstaff hurls an insult at Pistola, calling him a mountebank or cheap street performer. Derived etymologically from 'salta in banco' (one who climbs a bench to pitch snake oil).
Sir John, in questo intrigo non posso ac: Sir John, in this intrigue I cannot comply with you,

Sir John, in questo intrigo non posso ac.meaning: to comply with you / acquiesce (infinitive + enclitic 'vi')

Sir John, in questo intrigo non posso ac: Bardolfo joins the mutiny, politely stating he cannot participate in this scheme. The enclitic pronoun 'vi' is attached to infinitive 'accondiscendere' ('accondiscendervi': comply with you in this).
Bardolfo pauses theatrically before naming what prevents him from helping. The direct object clitic 'lo' anticipates the delayed subject 'L'onore' in line 55.
Bardolfo finishes his sentence: 'Honor forbids it'. The hypocrisy of a pickpocket citing 'honor' enrages Falstaff and sparks the famous monologue.
Ehi! paggio!: Disgusted by his men's sudden moral posturing, Falstaff calls over his page boy Robin to carry the letters instead.

Andate a impendervi,.meaning: to hang yourselves (archaic reflexive infinitive + enclitic 'vi')

Andate a impendervi,: Falstaff curses his followers to go hang themselves. Uses the archaic verb 'impendersi' (from Latin impendere, to hang oneself) with reflexive enclitic 'vi'.
ma non più a me!: A sharp comedic pun: Falstaff tells them to go hang themselves ('impendervi'), but to stop hanging upon or depending on him for money and lodging ('non più a me').
Two letters, take them, for two ladies.
Falstaff gives Robin the two identical love letters addressed to Alice and Meg. Imperative 'prendi' addressed to the page.
Consegna tosto, corri, via, lesto, va'!: Deliver quickly, run, away, nimble, go!
Falstaff orders the page to sprint off on the errand with a staccato barrage of imperatives: 'Consegna... corri... va''. 'Tosto' is an archaic adverb meaning 'swiftly / at once'.
L'onore!: Falstaff turns back to his henchmen with utter contempt, echoing the word 'Honor!' to begin his legendary monologue (adapted from Henry IV, Part 1, Act V, Scene 1).
Ladri! Voi state ligi all'onor vostro, v: Thieves! You stand bound to your honor, you!

Ladri! Voi state ligi all'onor vostro, v.meaning: you stand / remain (2nd person plural present)

Ladri! Voi state ligi all'onor vostro, v: Falstaff mocks the sheer absurdity of thieves pretending to be bound by knightly honor. Uses the doubled subject pronoun 'Voi... voi' for biting sarcasm, with 'ligi' meaning strictly obedient or bound.
Cloache d'ignominia, quando, non sempre,: Sewers of ignominy, when, not always, we
Falstaff calls them 'sewers of ignominy' (sinks of shame and filth), pointing out that even great gentlemen like himself cannot always remain bound to honor when survival is at stake.
possiam star ligi al nostro. Io stesso,: can stand bound to ours. I myself, yes, I, I,
Falstaff continues with comical self-importance ('I myself, yes, I, I!'): even he must sometimes bend the rules of honor. Apocopes 'possiam' and 'star'.
devo talor da un lato porre il timor di: must sometimes set aside the fear of God
Falstaff confesses that when money is scarce, he must occasionally set aside the fear of God. 'Porre da un lato' is an idiom meaning 'to set aside / discard'.
e, per necessità, sviar l'onore e usare: and, through necessity, dodge honor and use
Falstaff explains that necessity forces a gentleman to bypass honor. 'Sviar' is an apocope of 'sviare' (to detour around / deflect / sidetrack).
stratagemmi ed equivoci, destreggiar, bo: stratagems and equivocations, maneuver, tack to the wind.

stratagemmi ed equivoci, destreggiar, bo.meaning: to tack / beat against the wind (nautical metaphor)

stratagemmi ed equivoci, destreggiar, bo: Falstaff lists his survival tactics: stratagems, white lies, and deft maneuvering. 'Bordeggiare' is a nautical term meaning to tack back and forth against contrary winds, metaphorically describing clever dodging.
E voi, coi vostri cenci e coll'occhiata: And you, with your rags and with your crooked look
Falstaff contrasts his own gentlemanly necessity with his henchmen's squalor: they are dressed in rags ('cenci') with the shifty, treacherous squint ('occhiata torta') of predatory cutpurses.
da gattopardo: Falstaff finishes the description of their shifty look: 'like an ocelot / serval' ('da gattopardo'), predatory wildcats known for deceitful stealth.
e i fetidi sghignazzi, avete a scorta: and your foul sneers, have as your escort

Falstaff continues cataloging their repulsive traits: foul sneering laughter ('fetidi sghignazzi'). 'Avete a scorta' means 'you take as your guide and escort' (its direct object 'il vostro onor' follows in line 71).
il vostro onor! Che onore? che onor? che: your honor! What honor? what honor? what honor! what nonsense!
Falstaff's mocking diatribe reaches fever pitch: 'Your honor! What honor? what claptrap!'. 'Ciancia' is an expressive noun meaning empty chatter, gossip, or nonsense.
Che baia! Può l'onore riempirvi la panci: What a joke! Can honor fill your belly?

Falstaff's pragmatic catechism begins: can honor fill your empty belly? 'Che baia!' is a Tuscan idiom meaning 'What a joke! What nonsense!'. Directly translates Shakespeare's 'Can honour set to a leg? no'.
No. Può l'onor rimettervi uno stinco? No: No. Can honor set a shin for you? It cannot.

No. Può l'onor rimettervi uno stinco? No.meaning: to set / put back for you (infinitive + enclitic 'vi')

No. Può l'onor rimettervi uno stinco? No: Falstaff asks the questions and supplies the answers: can honor reset a broken shinbone? No, it cannot! ('rimettervi uno stinco').
Né un piede? No. Né un dito? No. Né un c: Nor a foot? No. Nor a finger? No. Nor a hair? No.
Falstaff continues his rapid catechism in a comedic diminuendo from foot down to a single hair, showing honor has zero physical or medical value.
L'onor non è chirurgo. Ch'è dunque? Una: Honor is not a surgeon. What is it then? A word.
Verbatim from Shakespeare: 'Honour hath no skill in surgery, then? no. What is honour? a word.' Falstaff dismisses honor as nothing more than an empty utterance.
Che c'è in questa parola? C'è dell'aria: What is in this word? There is air that flies.
Shakespeare asked 'What is that honour? air.' Boito poetically expands this into 'dell'aria che vola' (air that flies away and vanishes on the wind).
Bel costrutto! L'onore lo può sentire ch: Fine outcome! Can he who is dead feel honor?

Falstaff's sarcastic summary: 'A fine profit/reckoning!' (translating Shakespeare's 'A trim reckoning!'). He asks if dead men can feel honor, using clitic left dislocation ('L'onore lo può sentire...').
No. Vive sol coi vivi?... Neppure: perch: No. Does it live only with the living?... Not even that: because wrongly
Falstaff continues Shakespeare's catechism: honor doesn't live with the dead, nor can it survive among the living ('Vive sol coi vivi?... Neppure'), because human malice constantly attacks it.
lo gonfian le lusinghe, lo corrompe l'or: flatteries puff it up, pride corrupts it,
Falstaff explains why honor cannot survive even among the living: flattery inflates it with vanity, and arrogant pride corrupts it. Clitic direct object 'lo' refers back to honor.
l'ammorban le calunnie; e per me non ne: calumnies infect it; and as for me, I want none of it!

l'ammorban le calunnie; e per me non ne.meaning: as for me / for my part

l'ammorban le calunnie; e per me non ne: Falstaff concludes his philosophical catechism: slander and gossip infect honor like a plague ('ammorban'), so he wants nothing to do with it (translating Shakespeare's 'Therefore I'll none of it').
Ma, per tornare a voi, furfanti, ho atte: But, to return to you, rascals, I have waited too long.
Having demolished the abstract concept of honor, Falstaff turns back to his real business: punishing his mutinous henchmen ('furfanti' = rascals).

E vi discaccio..meaning: I drive out / banish / expel (1st person singular present)

Falstaff pronounces their formal banishment and expulsion: 'And I drive you out!'. Present indicative of 'discacciare' with direct object 'vi'.

al galoppo! Il capestro assai bene vi st: at a gallop! The halter suits you very well.

Falstaff shouts that the hangman's noose ('il capestro') suits them perfectly, as hanging is the proper fate for thieves who betray their master. 'Stare bene a qualcuno' is an idiom meaning 'to suit/become someone'.
Ladri! Via! Via di qua! Via di qua! Via: Thieves! Away! Out of here! Out of here! Out of here!

Ladri! Via! Via di qua! Via di qua! Via.meaning: out of here / away from here

Ladri! Via! Via di qua! Via di qua! Via: With furious blows of the broom, Falstaff drives Bardolfo and Pistola out into the street ('Via di qua!': 'Out of here!'), triumphantly ending Act 1 Scene 1.
Meg Page calls out cheerfully to greet her friend Alice Ford outside Ford's house in Windsor.
Alice springs her trap, naming Meg Page—the very woman to whom Falstaff sent a carbon-copy love letter.
Meg greets Alice's young daughter Nannetta.

Escivo appunto..meaning: I was going out / coming out (imperfect indicative)
just / precisely / at this exact moment

'Escivo' is an archaic and literary variant of 'uscivo' (first-person singular imperfect of 'uscire'). Alice explains she was just stepping outside to find Meg.
Alice explains her purpose: she was heading over specifically to share a laugh with Meg over the ridiculous letter she received.

The idiom 'in buon punto' means at the very right moment, opportune time. Alice welcomes their arrival just as she was seeking them out.

Meg immediately matches Alice's opening, revealing that an identical shocking incident has befallen her.
Che?: Mrs. Quickly's sharp interjection, intensely curious to hear the gossip.

Ti pare?.meaning: it seems / appears (3rd person singular present)
do you think so? / as if! / of course not!

Ti pare?: Idiomatic conversational retort 'Ti pare?' expressing mock indignation at the thought that Meg could ever betray a secret ('As if!').

'Oibò!' is a vigorous archaic interjection of protest or shock. Mrs. Quickly addresses Alice with the polite plural 'Vi pare?'.

in the / into the (articulated preposition nei)

propositi del diavolo, sarei: designs of the devil, I would be
Continuation of Alice's conditional protasis ('rei propositi del diavolo' = evil designs of the devil) leading to the apodosis with conditional 'sarei'.
promossa al grado di cavalleressa!: promoted to the rank of knight's lady!
'Cavalleressa' is Boito's mock-chivalric feminine title formed from 'cavaliere' (knight). Alice mocks Falstaff's boastful proposal to elevate her to a knight's companion.

to jest / make witty remarks / banter

'Motteggiare' means to banter, tease, or speak in jest. Alice cannot believe Meg could have had the same experience.

for here we are wasting the sunlight.

«amor bramo»..meaning: I crave / yearn for / passionately desire

Alice holds both letters side-by-side, pointing out the only swapped word.
È tal e quale:: 'Tal e quale' is an idiomatic Italian expression for an exact, indistinguishable replica.

«Non domandar perché, ma dimmi:».meaning: to ask (apocope of infinitive used as negative imperative)

«Non domandar perché, ma dimmi:»: Falstaff's imperious romantic prose: negative imperative 'Non domandar' followed by imperative with enclitic 'dimmi'.

Meg reflects on the bizarre coincidence. 'Pur strano' uses 'pur' as an intensifier meaning 'truly' or 'indeed'.

Mrs. Quickly proposes a methodical, cool-headed examination of the physical evidence. 'Flemma' refers to the ancient humor of phlegm, denoting unruffled calmness.

Alice checks the ink: written with the exact same batch.

Nannetta inspects the wax seal: impressed with the very same knightly crest ('stemma').

of beautiful woman and of man"...

«appariscente»: The comic climax of Falstaff's vanity: he describes his gargantuan, waddling frame as 'appariscente' (striking / handsome).

come una stella sull'immensità.»: like a star upon the immensity."

Mostro!: Quickly gasps in comic horror at Falstaff's audacity.

Dobbiam gabbarlo..meaning: we must / have to (apocope of dobbiamo)
to trick him / fool him (gabbare + clitic lo)

'Gabbare' is the classic Tuscan verb for playing a practical joke or beffa on someone. Alice decrees that Falstaff must be punished.
And make a great uproar of it.

E farne chiasso..meaning: to make of it (fare + clitic ne)
to cause a sensation / make a great fuss

Nannetta wants to make a public racket and spectacle of the trick ('farne chiasso').
And turn him into a laughingstock.

E metterlo in burletta..meaning: to put him / turn him (mettere + clitic lo)
to turn into a joke / make fun of

'Mettere in burletta' means to turn something into a laughingstock or comic farce (diminutive of 'burla', practical joke).
Oh! Oh! che spasso!: Nannetta exclaims in sheer delight at the prospect of the prank.
Che allegria!: Quickly joins the chorus of glee.
Che vendetta!: Meg savors the delicious vengeance they will exact on the insolent fat knight.
Insieme: Performance direction in the score marking the ensemble whispering passage between Ford, Dr. Caius, Bardolfo, and Pistola.
Quell'otre, quel tino!: Alice initiates the dazzling, rapid-fire staccato ensemble, comparing Falstaff's gigantic girth to a leather wineskin ('otre') and a wine-making vat ('tino').
Quel re delle pance,: Falstaff is hailed derisively as 'king of bellies', mocking his own royal monologue on his paunch from Act 1 Scene 1.
ci ha ancora le ciance: 'Ciance' denotes frivolous flirtatious chatter or coquettish sweet talk. Alice mocks that this mountain of lard still affects youthful seductions.
'Vagheggino' (from 'vagheggiare', to ogle or woo lovingly) is an ironic term for an effeminate dandy or conceited flirt.

E l'olio gli sgocciola: Boito captures Shakespeare's earthy description of Falstaff sweating grease ('oil drips from him'). Dative 'gli' functions as a dative of disadvantage.
dall'adipe unticcio: 'Unticcio' is a pejorative diminutive of 'unto' (greasy, oily). 'Adipe' is the anatomical term for bodily fat.
e ancor ei ne snocciola: 'Snocciolare' literally means to stone/pit fruit or shell peas, and idiomatically means to reel off verses, rhymes, or lies with effortless speed.
la strofa e il bisticcio!: 'Bisticcio' in literary Italian signifies an intricate pun, play on words, or rhyming assonance (such as 'gaia comare / compar gaio').
Lasciam ch'ei le pronte: Let us let him his ready

Lasciam ch'ei le pronte.meaning: let us allow / let (hortative, apocope of lasciamo)

Lasciam ch'ei le pronte: Hortative subjunctive construction: 'Lasciam ch'ei... spifferi' (Let us let him blurt out...). Enjambs with the following line.

sue ciarle ne spifferi;.meaning: blurt out / spill / babble (present subjunctive 3rd singular)

sue ciarle ne spifferi;: 'Spifferare' colloquially means to spill the beans or blurt out secrets recklessly. Governed by subjunctive after 'lasciam che'.
farà come i pifferi: he will fare like the pipers

First half of the famous Italian proverb: 'Fare come i pifferi di montagna, che andarono per suonare e furono suonati' (To do like the mountain pipers, who went to play music and ended up getting a beating).
who came down from the mountain.

che sceser dal monte..meaning: descended / came down (passato remoto 3rd plural, apocope of scesero)

Completes the proverb: Falstaff thought he was descending from on high to conquer the Windsor wives, but he will end up thoroughly beaten and humiliated.

Vedrai che se abbindolo.meaning: I bamboozle / ensnare / swindle (1st person singular present)

Vedrai che se abbindolo: 'Abbindolare' derives from 'bindolo' (skein-winder/pulley), meaning to wrap someone round one's finger or dupe them completely.
quel grosso compar,: Alice refers sarcastically to Falstaff's line ('il compar gaio') as 'quel grosso compar' (that huge crony).
più lesto d'un guindolo: 'Guindolo' is a revolving yarn-winder or reel. The comparative 'più lesto d'un guindolo' means faster than a spinning wheel.

lo faccio girar..meaning: to spin / turn round (apocope of girare)

Causative structure 'far girare' (to spin around like a top / make someone lose their head). Truncated infinitive 'girar' for meter and rhyme.
Quell'uom è un cannone,: Meg sings in simultaneous counter-melody, comparing Falstaff's explosive, bulky persona to a heavy siege cannon.
if it explodes, it finishes us off.
'Spacciare' idiomatically means to finish off, kill, or ruin someone completely. If Falstaff explodes like a cannon, all around him are doomed.
Colui, se l'abbraccia,: That fellow, if he hugs her,

Colui, se l'abbraccia,.meaning: embraces her / hugs her (elided la + abbraccia)

Colui, se l'abbraccia,: 'Colui' conveys contemptuous dismissal ('that creature'). 'L'abbraccia' has the elided direct object pronoun 'la' referring to any prospective lover.

ti schiaccia Giunone..meaning: Juno (queen of the gods, archetype of majestic womanhood)

Meg uses the ethical dative 'ti' to make the statement vivid. Juno, the majestic queen of Olympus, would be squashed flat under Falstaff's colossal embrace.

quel mostro si spappola.meaning: turns to mush / squashes into pulp / melts away

quel mostro si spappola: 'Spappolarsi' is a vivid, visceral Italian verb meaning to disintegrate into pulp or mush (from 'pappa', soft food/mash).
e perde il suo senno: 'Perdere il senno' is the classic literary idiom for losing one's reason or sanity (echoing Orlando's madness in Ariosto).
Falstaff will rush headlong into the trap laid for him by the merry wives.

sorriso di donna!: Completes the phrase: 'Potenza d'un fragile sorriso di donna!' (The power of a woman's frail smile!).

movenza di gonna!: 'Movenza di gonna' evokes the tantalizing, flirtatious rustle and movement of a woman's dress.

Se il vischio lo impegola.meaning: tars / entangles / traps (3rd person singular present)

Se il vischio lo impegola: Metaphor drawn from fowling: 'vischio' (sticky birdlime) and 'impegolare' (to smear with pitch/tar, trapping a bird so it cannot fly away).

lo udremo strillar..meaning: to shriek / squawk / squeal (apocope of strillare)

Acoustic imagery of Falstaff squealing like a trapped beast or stuck pig when caught in the wives' trap. Truncated infinitive 'strillar' for rhyme.

heat / rut / lustful itch / frantic desire

to vanish into smoke / evaporate / flare up

to conduct it / carry it out (condurre + clitic la)
it (direct object clitic referring to 'la burla')

Conviene condurla: Impersonal 'conviene' ('it is fitting/necessary') governs the infinitive 'condurre' combined with the enclitic direct object pronoun 'la' referring back to 'la burla' (the prank).
Nannetta warns that their practical joke must be engineered with intelligence ('senno') and theatrical craftsmanship ('arte') so Falstaff will not suspect a thing.

sapremo adoprar,: 'Sapremo adoprar' (future of 'sapere' expressing capability/know-how + apocopated infinitive of 'adoperare'). Rhymes with 'adoprar' / 'sudar'.
