gittò sulla rena.meaning: cast / threw / flung (passato remoto 3rd person singular)

gittò sulla rena: 'Gittò' is the archaic/poetic variant of 'gettò' (cast, hurled). 'Rena' (from Latin 'arena') is classic Tuscan and poetic Italian for beach sand.
di Windsor codesta: 'Codesta' is the specific Tuscan demonstrative adjective designating something near the addressee, modifying 'vorace balena' in the following line.
Completes Quickly's comic marine imagery: Falstaff is a ravenous whale ('vorace balena') stranded on the sandy shores of Windsor.
Ma qui non ha spazio: But here he has no room
'Non ha spazio' (he has no room). Mrs. Quickly notes that Windsor provides no room for Falstaff to expand his girth or indulge his gluttony.

da farsi più pingue;.meaning: to make oneself / become (fare + reflexive si)

da farsi più pingue;: Purpose infinitive clause 'da farsi' ('to make himself'). 'Pingue' is a Latinate, high-register poetic adjective for fat/fleshy, used with comic irony.
ne fecer già strazio: 'Fare strazio di' is an idiom meaning to butcher, tear apart, or make mincemeat of. 'Fecer' is the poetic apocope of 'fecero', and 'ne' refers back to Falstaff.
The subject of 'fecer già strazio': the sharp, articulate tongues of the Windsor women. Italian determiner syntax: 'le vostre tre lingue'.
Tre lingue più allegre: Quickly compliments the women's razor-sharp banter with musical and ornithological similes ('più allegre d'un trillo di nacchere').
d'un trillo di nacchere,: 'Nacchere' are castanets; 'un trillo di nacchere' evokes rapid rhythmic clicking, comparing their chattering speed to percussive castanets.
che spargon più chiacchiere: 'Spargon' is the apocopic 3rd person plural present of 'spargere' (to scatter, broadcast). 'Chiacchiere' means playful chatter or gossip.
'Cingallegre' is Boito's dialectal/archaic variant of 'cinciallegre' (great tits / chickadees), known for their tireless chirping. Creates a triple sdrucciolo rhyme with 'nacchere' and 'chiacchiere'.

Tal sempre s'esilari.meaning: such / so / in such manner (apocope of tale)
may cheer / gladden itself (present subjunctive 3rd person)

Tal sempre s'esilari: Optative subjunctive 's'esilari' (from 'esilarare/esilararsi', to cheer up, exhilarate). 'Tal' (apocope of 'tale') acts adverbially ('thus / in such a manner').
'Cinguettar' is the substantivized apocopic infinitive of 'cinguettare' (to chirp like birds, to twitter, to chat amiably). Subject of 's'esilari'.

Così soglion l'ilari.meaning: the cheerful / the merry (plural adjective with elided article)

Così soglion l'ilari: 'Soglion' is the apocopic 3rd person plural of 'solere' (to be accustomed / wont to). 'L'ilari' modifies 'comari' in the next line, echoing Shakespeare's title 'The Merry Wives'.
'Comari' translates Shakespeare's 'gossips' or 'merry wives'. 'Ciarlar' is an apocopic infinitive dependent on 'soglion': 'Così soglion l'ilari comari ciarlar' ('Thus are the merry wives wont to chatter').
Mr. Ford, Dr. Cajus, Fenton, Bardolfo, P: Mr. Ford, Dr. Caius, Fenton, Bardolfo, Pistol enter from the right,
Stage direction indicating the entrance of the male faction from stage right as the women withdraw.
while the Women exit from the left.

mentre le Donne escono da sinistra..meaning: they exit / go out (3rd person plural present)

Stage direction: the women exit stage left, maintaining the strict comic dichotomy between the two simultaneous conspiracies against Falstaff.
Ford nel centro, Pistola al suo fianco d: Ford in the center, Pistol at his right side,
Stage direction specifying scenic blocking: Ford stands center stage, flanked on either side by Falstaff's treacherous former henchmen.
Bardolfo al suo fianco sinistro, Fenton: Bardolfo at his left side, Fenton and Dr. Caius behind Ford.
Stage direction detailing the menacing physical encirclement of Ford by the agitators, each trying to whisper in his ear.
Tutti in gruppo parlando a Ford a bassa: All in a group speaking to Ford in a low voice and grumbling.

Tutti in gruppo parlando a Ford a bassa.meaning: in a low voice / in an undertone

Tutti in gruppo parlando a Ford a bassa: Stage direction establishing the conspiratorial, buzzing vocal texture of the male ensemble, whispering darkly to inflame Ford's jealousy.
È un ribaldo, un furbo, un ladro,: He is a rogue, a trickster, a thief,
Dr. Caius bursts out with his catalog of epithets against Falstaff, resuming his violent indignation from Act 1 Scene 1.
un furfante, un turco, un vandalo;: a scoundrel, a Turk, a vandal;
In traditional Italian idiom, 'un turco' or 'un vandalo' designates an unprincipled brute devoid of civility or pity. Sdrucciolo rhyme with 'scandalo'.
l'altro dì mandò a soqquadro: the other day he threw into turmoil

l'altro dì mandò a soqquadro.meaning: threw into turmoil / turned upside down / ransacked

l'altro dì mandò a soqquadro: 'L'altro dì' means 'the other day'. The idiom 'mandare a soqquadro' means to turn completely upside down, ransack, or wreak chaos upon.
my house and it was a scandal.
Caius reminds Ford of Falstaff's violent break-in at his home. 'Scandalo' completes the sdrucciolo rhyme with 'vandalo'.
Se un processo oggi gl'intavolo: If a lawsuit today I initiate against him

Se un processo oggi gl'intavolo.meaning: I initiate / table / set in motion (1st person singular present)
against him / to him (dative clitic gli elided)

Se un processo oggi gl'intavolo: 'Intavolare un processo' is an Italian legal idiom meaning to institute legal proceedings or file formal charges. 'Gl'' is the elided dative pronoun 'gli'.
he will pay for his robberies.

sconterà le sue rapine..meaning: he will pay for / expiate / serve time for (3rd person singular future)

'Scontare' means to expiate, serve a sentence, or pay the penalty for a crime. Italian determiner syntax: 'le sue rapine' = 'his robberies'.
Ma la sua più degna fine: Relative superlative 'la sua più degna fine' ('his most deserved end'). Caius moves from legal justice to apocalyptic damnation.
may be to go into the hands of the devil.

sia d'andare in man del diavolo..meaning: may it be / let it be (present subjunctive 3rd person singular)

Subjunctive of imprecation: 'sia d'andare in man del diavolo' ('let it be to fall into the clutches of the devil'). 'Man' is the apocopic form of 'mano'.
E quei due che avete accanto: And those two whom you have beside you
Caius points suspicion directly at Bardolfo and Pistola, warning Ford that they are just as untrustworthy as Falstaff.
gente sono di sua tribù,: Inverted syntax: '[essi] gente sono di sua tribù' ('they are people of his pack'). 'Tribù' is used pejoratively to denote Falstaff's criminal retinue.
non son due stinchi di santo: they are not two shins of a saint

non son due stinchi di santo.word: non son due stinchi di santo
non son due stinchi di santo.lemma: non essere uno stinco di santo
non son due stinchi di santo.meaning: to be no saints / to be far from virtuous

non son due stinchi di santo: Classic Italian idiom: 'non essere uno stinco di santo' (to be no saint / no angel). Derives from venerating saints' shinbones as sacred relics; applied here with barbed comedy to the two rogues.
Parallel metaphorical idiom: 'non essere un fiore di virtù' (to be far from a paragon of virtue), reinforcing Caius's contempt for Bardolfo and Pistola.
Falstaff, sì ripeto, giuro,: Falstaff, yes I repeat, I swear,
Bardolfo talks over Dr. Caius, swearing emphatically with 'ripeto, giuro' to convince Ford that his betrayal of Falstaff is motivated by genuine goodwill.

contro voi, John Falstaff rumina.meaning: ruminates / broods over / meditates (3rd person singular present)

contro voi, John Falstaff rumina: 'Ruminare' literally means to chew the cud; metaphorically it means to hatch, brood over, or chew on a sinister scheme.
Bardolfo's hypocritical euphemism: 'un progetto alquanto impuro' politely describes Falstaff's lustful ambition to seduce Ford's wife.
Son uom d'arme e quell'infame: I am a man of arms and that scoundrel
Bardolfo ridiculously wraps himself in military chivalry: 'Son uom d'arme' ('I am a man-at-arms'). 'Infame' refers to his former master Falstaff.
no longer do I want to drag you into the mire.

più non vo' che v'impozzangheri..meaning: drag into mud / besmirch with puddles (present subjunctive)

A brilliant neologism by Arrigo Boito: 'impozzangherare' (from 'pozzanghera', mud puddle), meaning to splash with mud, drag into the gutter, or besmirch someone's reputation. Governed by subjunctive.
Non vorrei, no, escir dai gangheri: I would not wish, no, to go off the hinges

Non vorrei, no, escir dai gangheri.meaning: I would wish / I would want (1st person singular conditional)
to go off the hinges / lose one's moral bearings
to go out (archaic variant of uscire, apocope)

Non vorrei, no, escir dai gangheri: 'Uscire dai gangheri' literally means to come off the door hinges (figuratively to lose control or deviate from proper conduct). Bardolfo poses as a paragon of uprightness.
dell'onor per un reame!: Completes Bardolfo's vow: he would not step off the hinges of honor for an entire kingdom. The grandiose Shakespearean bombast is hilariously out of place for a petty thief.
Messer Ford, l'uomo avvisato: Bardolfo quotes the first half of the Italian proverb: 'Uomo avvisato, mezzo salvato' ('Forewarned is forearmed', literally 'A forewarned man is half saved').
Completes the proverb: being warned is not enough ('non è salvo che a metà')—Ford must take active counter-measures.
Tocca a voi d'ordir l'agguato: It is up to you to plot the trap

Tocca a voi d'ordir l'agguato.meaning: it is the turn of / it is up to
to weave / plot / frame (apocope of ordire)

Tocca a voi d'ordir l'agguato: 'Toccare a' is an idiomatic verb phrase meaning 'it falls upon / it is the duty of someone'. 'Ordir' is apocopic for 'ordire'.

che l'agguato stornerà..meaning: will avert / ward off / deflect (3rd person singular future)

Wordplay on 'agguato' (ambush/trap): setting a counter-trap to foil Falstaff's original trap ('stornare' = to divert, ward off, neutralize).
Se parlaste uno alla volta: If you were to speak one at a time

Se parlaste uno alla volta.meaning: you spoke / you were to speak (2nd person plural imperfect subjunctive)

Se parlaste uno alla volta: Ford attempts to restore order among the babble of competing voices. The imperfect subjunctive 'se parlaste' begins a conditional period.
forse allor v'intenderò: perhaps then I will understand you

forse allor v'intenderò.meaning: then / in that case (apocope of allora)
I will understand (1st person singular future)

forse allor v'intenderò: 'Intenderò' (from 'intendere', to comprehend/understand). 'Allor' is the apocopic form of 'allora'.
Sir John Falstaff già v'appresta,: Sir John Falstaff is already preparing for you,
Pistola cuts in with his distinctive bombastic, pseudo-tragic cadence, addressing Ford with ominous portents.
Direct object of 'appresta'. 'Pericolo' establishes the dactylic (sdrucciolo) rhyme scheme with 'perpendicolo'.
Già vi pende sulla testa: Already there hangs over your head

Già vi pende sulla testa.meaning: over you / to you (dative of reference)

Già vi pende sulla testa: 'Pendere sulla testa' echoes the sword of Damocles, but here serves as a dark comic allusion to cuckold's horns sprouting on Ford's brow.
'A perpendicolo' means vertical or perpendicular (like a plumb line). Pistola hilariously depicts the cuckold's horns sticking straight up from Ford's head.
Messer Ford, fui già un armigero: Master Ford, I was once a squire
Pistola elevates his former status as Falstaff's lackey into the noble chivalric role of 'armigero' (squire/shield-bearer). Sdrucciolo rhyme with 'morigero'.
di quell'uom dall'ampia cute;: of that man of ample hide;
'Dall'ampia cute' (of vast skin/hide) is Boito's grotesque anatomical description of Falstaff's mountainous bulk.
or mi pento e mi morigero: now I repent and reform my conduct

or mi pento e mi morigero.meaning: I reform my manners / live temperately (1st person singular present)

or mi pento e mi morigero: 'Morigerarsi' is an erudite Latinism meaning to regulate one's conduct, become moral and temperate. Pistola claims to have turned over a new moral leaf.
The punchline to Pistola's 'moral conversion': he reformed solely 'per ragioni di salute' (to preserve his own skin after Falstaff threatened him with a broomstick).
La minaccia or v'è scoperta,: The threat now is uncovered to you,

La minaccia or v'è scoperta,.meaning: uncovered / revealed (past participle as predicate adjective)

La minaccia or v'è scoperta,: 'V'è scoperta' = 'vi è scoperta' (is laid bare / revealed to you). Pistola dramatically concludes his disclosure.
now known to you is the swindler.
'Ciurmador' (apocopic form of 'ciurmatore') denotes a deceitful mountebank or snake-oil charlatan who bewitches the gullible.
State all'erta, all'erta, all'erta!: Stay on guard, on guard, on guard!

State all'erta, all'erta, all'erta!.meaning: on guard / on the alert / on watch

State all'erta, all'erta, all'erta!: 'Stare all'erta' is a military watchman's warning meaning to keep sharp lookout (from 'erta', steep elevated ground). Repeated thrice for frantic urgency.
Here it is a question of honor.

Qui si tratta dell'onor..meaning: is a matter / concerns (3rd person singular present)
it is a question of / it concerns

Pistola uses the impersonal idiom 'si tratta di' (it is a question of / it concerns). The ultimate irony: Falstaff's discharged thug moralizing about 'honor'.
Se volete io non mi perito: If you wish, I do not hesitate

Se volete io non mi perito.meaning: you wish / you want (2nd person plural present)
I hesitate / shrink back (1st person singular present)

Se volete io non mi perito: Young Fenton steps forward. 'Peritarsi' is an elevated literary verb meaning to scruple, hesitate, or hold back out of fear or bashfulness.

di ridurlo alla ragione.meaning: to reduce him / bring him (ridurre + clitic lo)

di ridurlo alla ragione: 'Ridurre alla ragione' is an idiom meaning to make someone see reason, bring someone to their senses, or subdue someone.
co' le brusche o co' le buone,: by harsh means or by good,
Classic Italian idiom 'con le buone o con le brusche' (by fair means or foul, gently or roughly). 'Co'' is the apocopic contraction of 'con'.
and pay him according to his desert.

e pagarlo al par del merito..meaning: equal to / on a par with / according to

'Pagare al par del merito' means to reward or punish someone strictly according to what they deserve. Sdrucciolo rhyme with 'perito'.
Mi dà il cuore e mi solletica: My heart gives me courage and it tempts me

Mi dà il cuore e mi solletica.meaning: gives courage / have the heart to
tickles / tempts / entices (3rd person singular present)

Mi dà il cuore e mi solletica: 'Dare il cuore' is an idiom meaning to feel bold enough or have the courage for a challenge. 'Solleticare' (literally to tickle) means to tantalize or excite the appetite.

di sfondar quella ventraia.meaning: to smash through / cave in / puncture (apocope of sfondare)

di sfondar quella ventraia: 'Ventraia' is a pejorative/augmentative derivative of 'ventre' (belly), evoking a repulsive, colossal paunch.
Boito's magnificent compound portmanteau: 'iperbolico' (hyperbolic, astronomical) + 'apoplettico' (apoplectic, suffused with blood). An 8-syllable sdrucciolo tour de force rhyming with 'solletica'.
Col consiglio o co' la spada: With counsel or with the sword
Fenton pledges to defend Ford's house both by intellectual strategy ('consiglio') and by chivalric combat ('spada').
se lo trovo al tu per tu,: if I catch him face to face,

se lo trovo al tu per tu,.meaning: face to face / man to man / in private encounter
I find / catch (1st person singular present)

se lo trovo al tu per tu,: 'Al tu per tu' (or 'a tu per tu') is a classic idiom meaning eye-to-eye, face-to-face, or in direct confrontation (speaking informally using 'tu').
o lui va per la sua strada: either he goes on his way
Correlative disjunction 'o... o...' ('either... or...'). 'Andare per la sua strada' means to walk away, leave town, or retreat.
or I assign him to Beelzebub.

o lo assegno a Belzebù..meaning: I assign / consign / dispatch (1st person singular present)

Fenton vows that if Falstaff does not flee, he will dispatch him straight to Satan ('Belzebù', Beelzebub).
Bewildered by the simultaneous shouting from all sides, Ford demands a clear, singular repetition of the allegations.

In due parole:.meaning: in short / in a nutshell / in two words

In due parole:: Pistola steps forward to deliver his punchy, staccato summary: 'In due parole' ('In two words' / in a nutshell).
l'enorme Falstaff vuole: Pistola sets up a devastating sequence of four rhyming infinitive clauses detailing Falstaff's criminal intent.
entrar nel vostro tetto,: Synecdoche: 'tetto' (roof) stands for the domestic home or household. 'Entrar' is apocopic.

beccarvi la consorte,.meaning: to peck / snatch / seduce (beccare + clitic vi)

beccarvi la consorte,: 'Beccare' literally means to peck like a bird, colloquially used here to mean snatch, seduce, or cuckold. 'Vi' is the dative of disadvantage ('from you').

sfondar la cassaforte.meaning: to smash open / break in / breach (apocope of sfondare)

sfondar la cassaforte: 'Sfondar la cassaforte' (to smash open the iron strongbox). Pistola highlights that Falstaff aims to plunder Ford's wealth as well as his marriage.

e sconquassarvi il letto..meaning: to shatter / smash to pieces / wreck (sconquassare + clitic vi)

'Sconquassare' means to shatter or batter into pieces. The visceral image of Falstaff wrecking Ford's marriage bed directly inflames Ford's tormenting jealousy.

Caspita!.meaning: good heavens! / gadzooks! / well I never!

Caspita!: Dr. Caius's classic mild exclamation of shock and outrage (an Italian euphemism for stronger expletives).

Quanti guai!.meaning: how many / what a lot of (exclamative)

Quanti guai!: Ford gasps in dismay as suspicion grips him: 'Quanti guai!' ('What a mountain of trouble!'). Exclamatory adjective 'quanti' + plural noun 'guai'.
Already he wrote her a note...
Bardolfo reveals the smoking gun: Falstaff has already dispatched a written love letter to Alice ('le scrisse un biglietto').
Ma quel messaggio abbietto: Pistola interrupts to sanctimoniously denounce the love letter as an 'abject message' ('messaggio abbietto'), claiming moral revulsion.

ricusai..meaning: I refused / rejected (passato remoto 1st person singular)

Pistola proudly claims that he refused to deliver Falstaff's love letter. Lowercase initial matches the original.

Ricusai..meaning: I refused / rejected (passato remoto 1st person singular)

Bardolfo echoes Pistola with identical words, claiming his own share of virtue. Uppercase initial matches the original.

Badate a voi!.meaning: watch out / beware / take care (2nd person plural imperative)
to watch out for / look after / beware of

Badate a voi!: Pistola delivers the final warning: 'Badate a voi!' (look to your own defense / beware!), setting Ford's obsessive jealousy ablaze.

Badate!.meaning: watch out / pay attention (2nd person plural imperative)
to pay attention / heed / be on guard

Badate!: Bardolfo urgently warns Ford to be on guard. Second-person plural imperative of 'badare' (to heed, watch out). Having been expelled by Falstaff for refusing to carry the letters on grounds of 'honor', Bardolfo cynically betrays his master to Ford for profit.

Falstaff le occhieggia tutte,.meaning: them (feminine plural direct object clitic pronoun)
ogles / casts amorous glances at (3rd person singular present)

Falstaff le occhieggia tutte,: Pistola chimes in to fuel Ford's anxiety. 'Occhieggiare' is a vivid frequentative verb formed from 'occhio' (eye), meaning to eye up or flirt with the eyes. The clitic 'le' refers to women in general, emphasizing Falstaff's indiscriminate lust.
che siano belle o brutte,: whether they be fair or foul,

che siano belle o brutte,.meaning: they be (present subjunctive 3rd person plural of essere)

che siano belle o brutte,: Subjunctive 'siano' introduced by correlative 'che... o...' expresses an alternative condition ('whether they are... or...'). Pistola paints Falstaff as a ravenous monster who spares no woman regardless of appearance.
'Pulzella' is an archaic, literary Italian word for an unmarried maiden (cognate with French 'pucelle'). 'Maritate' functions substantively for married women. The pairing underscores Falstaff's total disregard for social propriety.
La corona che adorna: Bardolfo begins a pompous, mythological circumlocution for cuckold's horns. Boito uses elevated poetic diction ('corona', 'chiome') in a mock-heroic vein to terrify the bourgeois Ford.

d'Atteòn l'irte chiome.meaning: Actaeon (mythological hunter transformed into a horned stag)

d'Atteòn l'irte chiome: Mythological allusion to Actaeon (Atteone), who was turned into a stag with antlers after seeing Diana bathing. Antlers are the classic Renaissance symbol of cuckoldry. 'Irte' describes the rough, bristling hair of the beast.

su voi già spunta..meaning: sprouts / buds / emerges (3rd person singular present)

Completes the sentence: 'La corona che adorna d'Atteòn l'irte chiome su voi già spunta'. 'Spuntare' evokes the physical sprouting of horns on Ford's forehead. Lowercase opening preserves the syntactic continuation.
Come: Ford, taken aback by Bardolfo's grandiose classical circumlocution, interrupts in confusion. His query carries over to the next line ('sarebbe a dir?').

sarebbe a dir?.meaning: what does that mean / that is to say?

sarebbe a dir?: The phrase 'sarebbe a dir' is an idiomatic expression meaning 'what is that supposed to mean?' or 'that is to say?'. 'Dir' is the standard apocope of infinitive 'dire'.

«Le corna.».meaning: horns (irregular feminine plural of masculine noun corno)
cuckold's horns / sign of a betrayed husband

«Le corna.»: Bardolfo drops the poetic mask and blurts out the blunt, taboo term: 'Le corna' (the horns of cuckoldry). Italian 'corno' has the irregular feminine plural 'corna' when referring to anatomical horns or cuckoldry.
Brutta parola!: Ford is visibly repulsed and shocked. 'Brutta parola' expresses his horror at the vulgar accusation of cuckoldry, touching the raw nerve of his latent jealousy.

Ha voglie.meaning: has (3rd person singular present of avere)

Ha voglie: Dr. Caius interjects to stoke Ford's fury, eager to take revenge on Falstaff for the burglary and insults of Scene 1. Enjambment carries into the next line ('voraci il cavaliere').
Inverted word order ('voglie voraci il cavaliere') gives rhetorical weight to 'voraci'. Caius paints Falstaff not just as an admirer, but as a predatory glutton.
I will watch over my wife.

Sorveglierò la moglie..meaning: I will keep under surveillance / watch over (1st person singular future)

Ford resolves to spy on his household. Note Italian syntax: 'la moglie' with definite article translates naturally into English with a possessive determiner ('my wife'). Ford's jealousy mirrors Shakespeare's Othello, but Verdi and Boito set it in a comedic, manic key.
I will watch over the master.

Sorveglierò il messere..meaning: I will keep under surveillance / watch over (1st person singular future)

Parallel structure with the preceding line. 'Messere' is an archaic Italian honorific (derived from French 'messire'), used here with bitter sarcasm toward Falstaff.
Salvar vo' i beni miei: I want to save my possessions

Salvar vo' i beni miei.meaning: I want (apocopated poetic form of voglio)

Salvar vo' i beni miei: Ford characteristically treats his wife and honor as personal property ('i beni miei'). 'Vo'' is the apocopated poetic form of 'voglio' (I want). Natural Italian determiner syntax 'i beni miei' -> 'my possessions'.
Ford sees Falstaff as an encroaching predator trying to consume his property. 'Altrui' is an invariable possessive modifier meaning 'of another' or 'other people's'.

È lui..meaning: is (3rd person singular present of essere)
he / him (3rd person masculine disjunctive pronoun)

Alice Ford spots her husband Ford approaching in the garden. In Italian, disjunctive 'lui' after the copula 'è' serves as the predicate pronoun ('it is he').

È lei..meaning: is (3rd person singular present of essere)
she / her (3rd person feminine disjunctive pronoun)

Dr. Caius spots Alice Ford across the garden. The simultaneous cross-reactions of the men and women create Verdi's intricate, kinetic ensemble counterpoint.

S'egli sapesse!....meaning: if (elided form of se before vowel)
knew / were to know (3rd person singular imperfect subjunctive)

Alice imagines the explosive catastrophe if Ford were to find out about Falstaff's love letter. Imperfect subjunctive 'sapesse' in an exclamatory protasis conveys apprehension of an unrealized event.
Guai!: Nannetta gasps in dread. 'Guai' (plural of 'guaio') functions as an alarming exclamation warning of ruinous consequences should Ford discover what has transpired.

Schiviamo i passi suoi..meaning: let us avoid / dodge (1st person plural present/imperative)

Alice urges the women to evade Ford's approach. 'Schivare' means to dodge, sidestep, or evade. 'I passi suoi' is a poetic metonymy for his steps or path.
Ford è geloso?: Meg Page asks Alice about Ford's temperament. Ford's jealousy is the driving engine of the comic subplot, setting up his impending disguised visit to Falstaff as 'Signor Fontana'.
Alice confirms Ford's suspicious nature with succinct, dry understatement: 'Assai' (exceedingly / very much so).
Mistress Quickly silences the women as the male conspirators cross their path in the garden. 'Zitto' functions as an urgent interjection commanding hush.
Alice, Meg, and Quickly exit from the left. Nannetta remains.

Alice, Meg e Quickly escono da sinistra..meaning: they exit / go out (3rd person plural present)
remains / stays behind (3rd person singular present)

Stage direction marking the strategic departure of the three older women, leaving young Nannetta behind in the Windsor garden.
Ford, Dr. Cajus, Bardolfo e Pistola esco: Ford, Dr. Caius, Bardolfo, and Pistola exit from the right. Fenton remains.

Ford, Dr. Cajus, Bardolfo e Pistola esco.meaning: they exit / go out (3rd person plural present)
remains / stays behind (3rd person singular present)

Ford, Dr. Cajus, Bardolfo e Pistola esco: Stage direction indicating that the male plotting faction exits stage right, leaving Fenton alone on stage with Nannetta. This sets the stage for their stolen lyric duet.
Fenton's hushed whisper as he beckons Nannetta the moment the adults leave. The whispering onomatopoeia 'pst' contrasts brilliantly with the bustling nine-part polyphony of the ensembles.
Nannetta's cautionary sibilant response, warning Fenton to be careful even as she yields to his presence.

Vien qua..meaning: come (2nd person singular imperative, apocopic form of vieni)

Nannetta quietly beckons Fenton into the room, looking for a private spot away from the commotion.

Taci..meaning: be quiet / hush (2nd person singular imperative)

Second-person singular imperative of 'tacere' (to be silent). Nannetta shushes Fenton playfully while leaning in close.

Che vuoi?.meaning: you want (2nd person singular present of volere)

Che vuoi?: Nannetta feigns ignorance, prompting Fenton to declare his romantic desire. 'Vuoi' is the second-person singular present of irregular verb 'volere'.
Fenton's ardent, direct request: 'Due baci' (two kisses). Verdi accompanies this motif with a soaring, pure lyrical phrase in the woodwinds and strings.
Prepositional phrase 'in fretta' functioning adverbially (quickly, in haste). Nannetta agrees, but warns him of the extreme danger of discovery.

Labbra di foco!.meaning: lips (irregular feminine plural of masculine noun labbro)
fire / flame / passion (poetic monophthong variant of fuoco)

Labbra di foco!: Nannetta begins a rapid exchange of poetic conceits. 'Foco' is the traditional Italian poetic monophthong for 'fuoco'. 'Labbra' is the irregular feminine plural of masculine 'labbro'.

Labbra di fiore!....meaning: lips (irregular feminine plural of masculine noun labbro)

Fenton answers her metaphor with floral imagery ('foco' / 'fiore'), continuing their lyrical stichomythia in rhyming quinari/senari.

Che il vago gioco.meaning: that / which (relative pronoun referring to lips)

Che il vago gioco: Relative clause describing their lips. 'Vago' in Italian lyric poetry conveys grace, beauty, and elusive charm. The sentence resolves in the next line ('sanno d'amore').

sanno d'amore..meaning: know / have the flavor of (3rd person plural present of sapere)
of (elided form of di before vowel)

Idiomatic construction 'sapere di' means both 'to know / have expertise in' and 'to taste / smell of' love. The lowercase opening marks the syntactic continuation from 'Che il vago gioco'.

Che spargon ciarle,.meaning: scatter / shed / diffuse (poetic apocope of spargono)

Che spargon ciarle,: Fenton continues the praise of Nannetta's lips. 'Spargon' is the poetic truncation of 'spargono' (they scatter). 'Ciarle' denotes sweet, innocent gossip and prattle.

che mostran perle,.meaning: pearls (feminine plural; poetic metaphor for white teeth)

che mostran perle,: Petrarchan poetic conceit where 'perle' (pearls) represents sparkling white teeth behind parted lips. 'Mostran' is apocopated from 'mostrano'.

belle a vederle,.meaning: to see them / behold them (infinitive vedere + clitic pronoun le)

belle a vederle,: Infinitive construction with enclitic direct object pronoun 'le' (referring to 'labbra'): 'vederle' (to see them). 'Belle a vederle' balances aesthetics with romantic passion.

dolci a baciarle!.meaning: to kiss them (infinitive baciare + clitic pronoun le)

dolci a baciarle!: Syntactic twin to the preceding line ('belle a vederle' / 'dolci a baciarle'), moving from sight to touch. The enclitic '-le' refers back to 'labbra'.

Labbra leggiadre!.meaning: lips (irregular feminine plural of masculine noun labbro)

Labbra leggiadre!: Fenton's rapturous exclamation. 'Leggiadro' is a quintessentially lyrical Italian adjective evoking elegance, courtly beauty, and lightness.

Man malandrine!.meaning: hands (poetic apocope of feminine plural mani)

Man malandrine!: Nannetta gently rebukes Fenton as his hands wander. 'Man' is the poetic apocope of feminine plural 'mani'. 'Malandrine' means roguish, crafty, or thieving.

Ciglia assassine!.meaning: eyelashes / brows (irregular feminine plural of masculine noun ciglio)

Ciglia assassine!: Fenton playfully invokes the Italian lyric trope of the lady's glance as a deadly weapon that slays the lover's heart. 'Ciglia' is an irregular feminine plural noun.
Pupille ladre!: Continuing the poetic duel of compliments: Nannetta's eyes steal his peace and heart. 'Pupille ladre' pairs rhythmically with 'ciglia assassine'.

T'amo!.meaning: I love you (clitic ti + 1st sing. present amo)

T'amo!: Fenton's passionate echo right as Ford turns around and catches them in the act.
Nannetta chides Fenton for his boldness in an open garden where her father could appear at any moment. Her tone is affectionate rather than angry.
Ford stubbornly denies his own foolishness.
Fenton insists on his prize ('due baci'), repeating his melodic plea with youthful persistence.

Basta..meaning: it suffices / that is enough (3rd person singular present)

Third-person singular present of impersonal verb 'bastare', used as an imperative command: 'That's enough!'

Mi piaci.meaning: you please / are pleasing (2nd person singular present)

Mi piaci: Italian indirect construction 'mi piaci' (literally 'you are pleasing to me', meaning 'I like you / I adore you'). The thought completes in the next line ('tanto!').
tanto!: Adverb of quantity modifying 'mi piaci' ('I like you so much!'). Lowercase reflects continuation from the previous line.

Vien gente..meaning: comes / is coming (apocopated 3rd person singular present of venire)

Nannetta senses footsteps approaching. 'Gente' is a collective feminine singular noun taking singular verb 'vien' (apocope of 'viene').
A kissed mouth does not lose its good fortune.
Fenton quotes the first half of Boccaccio's famous aphorism from Decameron (II, 7): 'Bocca baciata non perde ventura...'
Rather it renews itself as does the moon.
Nannetta enters singing offstage to complete Boccaccio's proverb ('...anzi rinnuova come fa la luna'), playfully asserting that kisses only enhance youthful beauty.
Falstaff has made a fool of me.

Falstaff m'ha canzonata..meaning: mocked / ridiculed / made sport of (feminine singular past participle)

Alice re-enters, indignant at Falstaff's insolent presumption. 'Canzonare' means to mock, ridicule, or dupe. The past participle 'canzonata' agrees in feminine singular with the preceding direct object clitic 'm''.
Meg agrees wholeheartedly. Falstaff's identical letters insulted both women's intelligence and dignity, requiring collective retribution.
What if I wrote him a line?...

Se gli scrivessi un rigo?....meaning: I wrote / were to write (1st person singular imperfect subjunctive)

Alice ponders baiting the trap with a letter. Imperfect subjunctive 'scrivessi' introduced by 'se' expresses a tentative suggestion ('What if I were to write him a line?').

Val meglio un'ambasciata..meaning: is worth / avails (apocopated 3rd person singular present of valere)

Nannetta astutely suggests an oral message via an emissary instead of a written note. 'Val meglio' is an idiomatic construction meaning 'it is better / more effective'. An oral message leaves no physical paper trail.

Da quel brigante.meaning: to / at (preposition denoting movement towards a person)

Da quel brigante: Alice turns to Mistress Quickly. Preposition 'da' with a person denotes going to someone's presence ('andare da qualcuno'). 'Brigante' characterizes Falstaff as an unscrupulous outlaw.
tu andrai. Lo adeschi all'offa: you shall go. You entice him with the bait

tu andrai. Lo adeschi all'offa.meaning: you will go (2nd person singular future)
you entice / lure / bait (present subjunctive / imperative 2nd person singular)

tu andrai. Lo adeschi all'offa: Alice commissions Quickly as their ambassador. 'Adescare' means to lure or hook with bait. 'Offa' is a classical literary word (from Latin 'offa', the honey-cake thrown to pacify Cerberus in Virgil and Dante), meaning a tempting bait or bribe.
d'un ritrovo galante: 'Ritrovo galante' designates an amorous rendezvous or secret tryst, tailored to exploit Falstaff's vanity and lust.
Completes the invitation: 'un ritrovo galante con me'. Alice fearlessly offers herself as the decoy for the trap.

Questa è gaglioffa!.meaning: this / this thing (demonstrative pronoun, feminine singular)

Questa è gaglioffa!: Mistress Quickly laughs in delight at the ruse. 'Gaglioffo' is a rich vernacular term meaning roguish, knavish, buffoonish, or rascal-like. Quickly loves the sheer cunning of the plot.
Che bella burla!: Nannetta cheers the plan. 'Burla' is the classic Italian literary term for a practical joke, directly evoking the merry spirit of Boccaccian novelle.
Prima,: Alice outlines the two steps of their plan: first stroke his ego, then humble him.

per attirarlo a noi,.meaning: to attract him / lure him (infinitive attirare + enclitic pronoun lo)

per attirarlo a noi,: Final infinitive clause of purpose: 'per attirarlo a noi'. The enclitic direct object pronoun '-lo' refers to Falstaff.

lo lusinghiamo, e poi.meaning: we flatter / entice / cajole (1st person plural present)

lo lusinghiamo, e poi: Alice recognizes that Falstaff's supreme vanity makes flattery ('lusingare') the perfect trap.
we give him a piece of our mind in rhyme.

gliele cantiamo in rima..meaning: them to him (combined clitic pronoun: indirect gli + feminine plural direct le)
we tell / sing (1st person plural present)
in rhyme / explicitly / thoroughly / in plain terms

Vivid Italian idiom 'cantarle a qualcuno' (literally 'to sing them to someone', meaning to speak frankly or tell someone off bluntly). Combined with 'in rima', it means to deliver a sharp rebuke in exquisite poetic form.
Mistress Quickly declares that Falstaff's crude insolence forfeits any claim to polite deference or chivalric respect ('riguardo').

È un bove..meaning: ox / castrated bull (poetic/archaic variant of bue)

Alice's blunt insult. 'Bove' evokes heavy, clumsy stupidity, and pointedly alludes to a horned animal, mocking the horn motif that Ford fears.
He is a man without faith.
Meg Page condemns Falstaff's utter lack of integrity ('senza fede'), having sent the identical love declaration word-for-word to two married women at once.
He is a mountain of lard.
Alice translates Prince Hal's classic insults from Shakespeare's Henry IV Part 1 into colorful Italian: 'a mountain of mummy' / 'huge hill of flesh' -> 'un monte di lardo'.
Meg reinforces the mock-judicial condemnation of Falstaff. 'Clemenza' is an elevated Latinate noun emphasizing that their prank will be merciless.
È un ghiotton che scialacqua: He is a glutton who squanders

È un ghiotton che scialacqua.meaning: squanders / dissipates / wastes lavishly (3rd person singular present)

È un ghiotton che scialacqua: Alice highlights Falstaff's voracious appetite. 'Ghiotton' (apocopated from 'ghiottone') means glutton; 'scialacquare' means to spend prodigally or waste assets on luxurious indulgence.
all his wealth on the cook.

tutto il suo aver nel cuoco..meaning: wealth / assets / possessions (substantivized infinitive of avere)

Substantivized infinitive 'aver' (apocope of 'avere') denotes accumulated wealth or substance ('his all'). Alice scoffs that every penny he possesses is consumed by his belly.
We will dunk him into the water.

Lo tufferem nell'acqua..meaning: we will plunge / dunk (poetic apocope of tufferemo)

Nannetta gleefully anticipates the climax of Act 2: pitching Falstaff out the window in the laundry basket into the river Thames! 'Tufferem' is the poetic truncation of future tense 'tufferemo'.
We will roast him at the fire.

Lo arrostiremo al fuoco..meaning: we will roast (1st person plural future)

Alice pairs Nannetta's water punishment with a culinary fire metaphor ('arrostiremo al fuoco'), playfully suggesting that the fat knight will be cooked like his own dinners.
Che gioia!: Nannetta's exuberant exclamation of youthful mirth at the prospect of humiliating Falstaff.

Procaccia di far bene.meaning: take care / strive / endeavor (2nd person singular imperative)
to do / make / perform (apocopated infinitive of fare)

Procaccia di far bene: Meg cautions Quickly to play her role convincingly. 'Procacciare di' + infinitive is a formal, elegant Italian expression meaning to take diligence or strive to accomplish a task.
Theatrical language ('la tua parte': your role) underscoring the comedy's play-within-a-play dynamics. Lowercase maintains syntax from the preceding line.

Chi viene?.meaning: comes / is coming (3rd person singular present of venire)

Chi viene?: Mistress Quickly sounds the alarm upon hearing footsteps approaching again in the garden.

Là c'è qualcun che spia..meaning: spies / is spying (3rd person singular present)

Meg catches sight of the men returning. 'C'è qualcun che spia' (there is someone spying) creates rapid dramatic suspense, prompting another quick exit.
Escono rapidamente da destra Alice, Meg,: Alice, Meg, and Quickly rapidly exit from the right. Nannetta remains,

Escono rapidamente da destra Alice, Meg,.meaning: they exit / go out (3rd person plural present of uscire)

Escono rapidamente da destra Alice, Meg,: Stage direction marking the quick exit of Alice, Meg, and Quickly, intentionally leaving Nannetta behind in the Windsor garden once again.
Stage direction noting Fenton instantly reappearing at Nannetta's side. The clitic 'le' functions as a dative of proximity with 'accanto' ('beside her').
Fenton reopens their flirtatious duel with a fencing metaphor. In Renaissance chivalric poetry, the assault ('assalto') is an established trope for romantic pursuit.
Nannetta matches Fenton's syntax and meter, framing their exchange as a playful 'gara' (contest of wits and kisses).
Ferisci!: Second-person singular imperative of 'ferire' (to strike or wound). Nannetta issues a spirited fencing challenge to Fenton.

Para!.meaning: parry! / ward off! (2nd person singular imperative)

Para!: Second-person singular imperative of 'parare' (to parry in fencing). Fenton lunges in for a kiss, daring her to defend herself.
Nannetta dodges with athletic grace: 'La mira è in alto' (the aim is high / aiming above the target), simultaneously hinting at the lofty purity of true love.
L'amor è un agile: Boito's lyric poetry sets this philosophical definition of love. 'Amor' is the poetic apocope of 'amore'. The metaphor continues into the following lines.
torneo, sua corte: Love is cast as a medieval tournament governed by a chivalric court of love ('sua corte'). Lowercase opening maintains the verse structure.

vuol che il più fragile.meaning: wills / wants (apocopated 3rd person singular present of volere)

vuol che il più fragile: 'Vuol che' introduces a subjunctive clause of chivalric ordinance. 'Il più fragile' represents the delicate maiden who nevertheless holds dominion in love.

vinca il più forte..meaning: vanquish / win / conquer (3rd person singular present subjunctive)

Present subjunctive 'vinca' governed by 'vuol che'. Boito crafts an exquisite Petrarchan paradox: in the court of love, the frailest woman vanquishes the strongest man.
I arm myself, and look upon you.

M'armo, e ti guardo..meaning: I arm myself (reflexive verb 1st person singular present)
I look at / gaze upon (1st person singular present)

Fenton accepts the challenge of the tournament. 'Armarsi' is used reflexively ('m'armo': I arm myself). Direct object clitic 'ti' precedes 'guardo' (I look at you).
I await you at the pass.

T'aspetto al varco..meaning: I await you (direct object clitic ti + aspetto)
to wait in ambush / await someone at a decisive pass

Idiomatic expression 'aspettare al varco' (literally to wait at a narrow pass or crossing), meaning to lie in wait for someone at the crucial juncture to catch them.
Classical emblem of Cupid's archery: the curving lip forms the bow ('l'arco') poised to loose the shaft of love.
And the kiss is the dart.
Fenton completes the emblematic conceit: if the curved lip is the bow, the kiss itself is the arrow ('il dardo') that strikes home.
Bada! la freccia: Fenton playfully warns Nannetta of his oncoming kiss, extending the lyrical archery duel ('Il labbro è l'arco / E il bacio è il dardo'). Verdi sets their intimate love duet in soaring, flexible lyricism that sparkles within the surrounding comic intrigue.

fatal già scocca.meaning: shoots forth / is loosed (3rd sing. present)

fatal già scocca: Poetic apocope 'fatal' from 'fatale'. 'Scoccare' describes an arrow springing from a bowstring, here signifying Fenton's eager kiss aimed at Nannetta's tresses.
dalla mia bocca: Preposition 'da' combines with feminine definite article 'la' into 'dalla'. The arrow of passion originates from Fenton's own mouth.
Articulated preposition 'su' + 'la' = 'sulla'. Fenton seals his poetic archery challenge by planting a kiss squarely upon Nannetta's hair.

Eccoti avvinto..meaning: here you are (presentative ecco + clitic ti)

Presentative adverb 'ecco' merges with the 2nd-person clitic pronoun 'ti'. Nannetta wittily turns Fenton's combat metaphor around, declaring him bound fast in her embrace ('avvinto', past participle of 'avvincere').

Chiedo la vita!.meaning: to beg for mercy / yield in combat

Chiedo la vita!: Fenton feigns knightly surrender: 'chiedere la vita' is traditional chivalric combat terminology used by a defeated knight yielding to his conqueror.

Io son ferita,.meaning: am (1st sing. present, apocope of sono)

Io son ferita,: Poetic apocope 'son' from 'sono'. Nannetta playfully acknowledges Cupid's dart, confessing she is wounded by his love even while holding mastery over him.
Contrastive conjunction 'ma' introduces the loving antithesis: though she is 'wounded', Fenton is utterly 'vanquished' ('vinto', irregular past participle of 'vincere').

Pietà! Facciamo.meaning: let us make / we make (1st plural hortative/present)

Pietà! Facciamo: Fenton cries for clemency ('Pietà!'). 'Facciamo' is 1st-person plural hortative subjunctive of 'fare', beginning the reconciliation idiom 'fare la pace'.
Completing the phrase 'facciamo la pace'. Fenton leaves the sentence suspended on 'e poi...' with teasing innuendo.
Se vuoi,: Conditional conjunction 'se' with 2nd-person singular present of 'volere'. Fenton makes his romantic proposal conditional upon Nannetta's consent.

ricominciamo..meaning: we begin again / let us restart (1st plural)

1st-person plural hortative/present indicative of 'ricominciare'. Fenton's playful terms of truce: immediately recommencing the game of kissing from scratch.
Bello è quel gioco: Fronted predicate adjective 'Bello' launching the popular Italian proverb: 'Bello è quel gioco che dura poco' (A game is good when it lasts but briefly).
Relative clause modifying 'quel gioco'. Nannetta wisely cautions that lingering too long in the garden risks discovery by her father and his companions.
Amor mio!: Poetic apocope 'amor' from 'amore'. Fenton breathes a tender exclamation of affection before being forced to separate.
Vien gente. Addio!: Apocope 'vien' from 'viene' with collective singular subject 'gente'. Nannetta hears approaching footsteps and urges a hasty parting.
Rientrano dal fondo Ford, Dr. Cajus, Bar: Ford, Dr. Caius, Bardolfo, Pistola re-enter from the back.
Stage direction indicating the return of the four male conspirators. Their brooding, jealous intrigue shatters the lyricism of the young lovers and resumes their counterplot against Falstaff.
Udrai quanta egli sfoggia: You shall hear how much he displays

Udrai quanta egli sfoggia.meaning: shows off / flaunts / displays (3rd sing. present)

Udrai quanta egli sfoggia: Bardolfo prepares Ford for their encounter at the Garter Inn. 'Udrai' is 2nd-person singular future of 'udire'. 'Sfoggiare' means to ostentatiously flaunt.
Direct object of 'sfoggia'. Boito's mock-heroic phrase portrays Falstaff's aristocratic pretensions and high-flown rhetorical vanity.
Diceste ch'egli alloggia: Ford addresses Bardolfo and Pistola with formal 2nd-person plural 'diceste' (passato remoto of 'dire'). 'Ch'egli' elides conjunction 'che' before 'egli'.
dove?: Ford's urgent, suspicious question demanding Falstaff's precise location in Windsor so he can confront the scoundrel in disguise.
Pistola names Falstaff's headquarters: The Garter Inn ('L'Osteria della Giarrettiera'). Articulated preposition 'a' + 'la' = 'alla'.
FORD A lui mi annuncerete,: FORD You shall announce me to him,

FORD A lui mi annuncerete,.meaning: you shall announce / introduce (2nd plural future)

FORD A lui mi annuncerete,: Ford's speech contains his character label in the libretto cue. He commands Bardolfo and Pistola to introduce him to Falstaff using the future indicative 'annuncerete' with imperative force.
ma con un falso nome;: Ford initiates his deceptive plan to adopt the disguise of 'Signor Fontana' (Shakespeare's Master Brook), probing Falstaff's intentions incognito.
poscia vedrete come: Literary adverb 'poscia' (from Latin postea). Ford confidently boasts to his accomplices that they will watch his trap snap shut upon Sir John.
I catch him in the net.
Hunting metaphor: 'pigliare nella rete'. Both Ford and Alice Ford separately envision catching Falstaff in a net, dramatizing the parallel comedic snares.

Ma... non una parola..meaning: a single / one (indefinite article used numerically)

Elliptical negative command enforcing strict silence. Ford warns his rogue accomplices that absolute secrecy is vital to his scheme.
I do not engulf myself in gossip.

In ciarle non m'ingolfo..meaning: I engulf myself / immerse myself (1st sing. present reflexive)

Reflexive verb 'ingolfarsi' (from golfo), meaning to plunge deeply into a gulf. Bardolfo swears he never drowns himself in frivolous talk ('ciarle').

Io mi chiamo Bardolfo..meaning: am called / am named (1st sing. present reflexive)

Bardolfo cites his own name as a roguish badge of honor and trustworthiness, creating a comic rhyming pair ('ingolfo' / 'Bardolfo').

Io mi chiamo Pistola..meaning: am called / am named (1st sing. present reflexive)

Pistola echoes Bardolfo in comedic parallel, rhyming with Ford's 'parola' to guarantee his own impenetrable silence.

Siam d'accordo..meaning: we are agreed / we are in accord

Dr. Caius eagerly seals the illicit pact and exits.
L'arcano: Direct object of 'custodirem' on the following line. 'Arcano' lends a mock-elevated, conspiratorial tone to their petty intrigue.

custodirem..meaning: we shall guard / keep safe (1st plural future, apocope)

Poetic apocope of the 1st-person plural future 'custodiremo' -> 'custodirem', fitting Boito's strict metrical scheme.

Son sordo.meaning: I am (1st sing. present, apocope of sono)
to be deaf and dumb / utterly discreet

Son sordo: Apocope 'son' from 'sono'. Pistola invokes the traditional idiom of absolute secrecy: being 'sordo e muto' (deaf and dumb).
Coordinating conjunction 'e' links the second adjective, completing Pistola's comic pledge that wild horses could not drag the secret out of him.
Ford confirms universal agreement among the men. The collective pronoun 'tutti' unites Ford, Dr. Caius, Bardolfo, and Pistola in a single conspiracy.

Qua la mano..meaning: to shake hands / seal an agreement

Elliptical colloquial idiom: 'Qua la mano!' ([Put] the hand here! / Shake hands!). Ford binds the conspirators through a physical handshake.
Si avanzano nel fondo Alice, Nannetta, M: Alice, Nannetta, Meg, Quickly advance in the background.

Si avanzano nel fondo Alice, Nannetta, M.meaning: they advance / move forward (3rd plural present)

Si avanzano nel fondo Alice, Nannetta, M: Crucial stage direction introducing the musical miracle of Act 1: the rapid-fire double nonet, contrasting the four laughing women in 6/8 with the five plotting men in 4/4.
Del tuo barbaro diagnostico: Dr. Caius pedantically offers medical analysis ('diagnostico'). Boito crafts Caius's strophe with triple sdrucciolo rhymes (diàgnostico / bàrbaro / òstico / rabàrbaro) to depict his comic pomposity.
perhaps the affliction is much less terrible.
Caius attempts to console Ford by suggesting that his suspected cuckoldry might not be as catastrophic as diagnosed. Apocope 'men' from 'meno'.
Ti convien tentar la prova: It behoves you to attempt the ordeal

Ti convien tentar la prova.meaning: it behoves / is fitting (apocope of conviene)

Ti convien tentar la prova: Impersonal verb 'convenire' taking dative clitic 'ti' ('ti convien', it is fitting for you). Apocopes: 'convien' and infinitive 'tentar'. Caius urges putting suspicion to the test.
Absolute superlative adjective 'molestissima' modifying 'prova'. 'Ver' is poetic apocope for 'vero' (the truth). To discover reality may hurt, but it is necessary medicine.
Così avvien col sapor ostico: So it happens with the harsh taste
Medical simile comparing unpleasant reality to bitter draughts. 'Ostico' denotes an acrid, disagreeable taste. Apocopes: 'avvien' (from avviene) and 'sapor' (from sapore).
del ginepro e del rabarbaro;: Caius cites classic bitter purgatives: juniper berry ('ginepro') and medicinal rhubarb root ('rabarbaro'). Sdrucciolo meter on 'rabàrbaro' rhyming with 'diàgnostico'.
il benessere rinnova: Syntactic inversion: 'il benessere' is direct object of 'rinnova', whose subject is 'l'amarissimo bicchier' in the following verse.
The bitter cup that restores health. 'Bicchier' is apocopated from 'bicchiere' to form a sharp tronco rhyme with 'ver'.

Voi dovete empirgli il calice,.meaning: to fill for him (empire + dative clitic gli)

Voi dovete empirgli il calice,: Modal 'dovete' governing compound infinitive 'empirgli' (archaic 'empire' for riempire + clitic 'gli', to him). Sdrucciolo rhymes: càlice / bàndolo / sàlice. Pistola advises making Falstaff drunk.

tratto, tratto, interrogandolo,.meaning: from time to time / now and then

tratto, tratto, interrogandolo,: Boito uses the rhythmic repetition 'tratto, tratto' (intermittently). 'Interrogandolo' combines present gerund with direct object clitic 'lo' in a four-syllable sdrucciolo cadence.
per tentar se vi riesca: in order to try whether you succeed
Purpose clause 'per tentar'. 'Riuscire' is used impersonally with dative pronoun 'vi' ('se vi riesca', whether you may succeed).
in finding the head of the tangle's thread.

di trovar del nodo il bandolo..meaning: to find the key / unravel a tangled mystery

Famous Italian idiom: 'trovare il bandolo della matassa' (finding the unraveling thread-end of the skein). Pistola advises Ford to extract the key confession from Sir John.
As the willow bends toward the water.
Poetic simile comparing the weeping willow drooping towards running water to Falstaff's natural, irresistible thirst for wine. Sdrucciolo noun 'sàlice'.
Completing the correlative simile: 'Come... Così...'. Apocopes: 'vin' from 'vino' and 'cavalier' from 'cavaliere', producing a brisk tronco rhythm.
Scoverete la sua tresca,: You will uncover his illicit intrigue,

Scoverete la sua tresca,.meaning: you will uncover (2nd plural future, archaic variant)

Scoverete la sua tresca,: 'Scoverete' is the archaic phonetic variant of 'scoprirete'. 'Tresca' specifically denotes a clandestine, adulterous intrigue.

scoprirete il suo pensier..meaning: you will discover / reveal (2nd plural future)

Rhetorical polyptoton pairing 'scoverete' with 'scoprirete'. 'Pensier' is apocopated from 'pensiero' to create a masculine tronco rhyme with 'cavalier'.
Tu vedrai se bene adopera: You shall see whether my art works well
Ford boasts of his cunning scheme to test Falstaff. Sdrucciolo rhymes: àdopera / òpera. 'Adoperare' functions intransitively meaning 'to take effect / operate effectively'.
Subject of 'adopera' from previous line. Ford designates Sir John with bitter venom as 'quell'infame', giving voice to his corrosive jealousy.
E sarà prezzo dell'opera: And it will be worth the effort
Classical idiom 'essere prezzo dell'opera' (worth the trouble / rewarding). Ford believes exposing Falstaff will abundantly repay his anxiety and outlay.
'Discopro' is a literary form of 'scopro' (from discoprire). 'Trame' (literally weavings) evokes the tangled web of Falstaff's seductive schemes.
Se su lui volgo il ridicolo: If upon him I turn ridicule
Sdrucciolo rhymes: ridìcolo / perìcolo. Ford intends to turn public derision back against Falstaff to cleanse his own wounded vanity.
we shall not have sweated in vain.

non avrem sudato invan..meaning: we shall have (1st plural future, apocope of avremo)

Double apocope: 'avrem' (from avremo) and 'invan' (from invano). 'Sudare' metaphorically signifies strenuous labor.
S'io mi salvo dal pericolo,: If I save myself from the danger,

S'io mi salvo dal pericolo,.meaning: I save myself (1st sing. present reflexive)

S'io mi salvo dal pericolo,: Reflexive verb 'salvarsi'. Ford views Sir John's attempted seduction as an existential threat to his household dignity.
Tuscan proverb: 'l'angue morde il cerretano' (the snake bites the snake-charmer / the trickster is bitten by his own reptile). Apocope 'cerretan' rhymes with 'invan'.

Messer Ford, un infortunio.meaning: Master / Sir (honorific title, apocope of messere)

Messer Ford, un infortunio: Bardolfo addresses Ford with feudal honorific 'Messer' (apocope of messere). Sdrucciolo rhymes: infortùnio / plenilùnio.
