Gli svampi l'uzzolo!.meaning: vanish in smoke / evaporate / burn out (3rd sing. present subjunctive)

Gli svampi l'uzzolo!: Optative subjunctive with dative clitic 'gli'. 'Uzzolo' is a colorful vernacular term for an amorous whim or persistent itch, which must be smoked out.

Pizzica, pizzica, l'unghia rintuzzola!.meaning: blunt / turn back / wear down (2nd sing. imperative)

Pizzica, pizzica, l'unghia rintuzzola!: Imperative 'rintuzzola' (frequentative of rintuzzare, to blunt or turn the edge). The tormentors are urged to pinch so violently that their nails turn back on his tough hide.
DR. CAJUS E FORD: Character heading for Dr. Caius and Master Ford stepping up to lead the rhythmic masculine litany of insults.

Cialtron!.meaning: scoundrel / rascal / shameless buffoon (apocope of cialtrone)

Cialtron!: Truncated insult ('Cialtron' for 'cialtrone'). Boito begins a dazzling chain of masculine augmentative nouns in -on hurled like hammer blows.

Poltron!.meaning: coward / sluggard / lazy knave (apocope of poltrone)

Poltron!: Insult branding Falstaff cowardly and indolent ('Poltron' for 'poltrone'), rhyming with 'Cialtron'.
Ghiotton!: Insult targeting Sir John's bottomless gluttony ('Ghiotton' for 'ghiottone').
TUTTI GLI UOMINI: Choral heading marking the full male chorus joining the barrage of rhythmic insults.

Pancion!.meaning: big belly / potbelly (augmentative of pancia, apocope of pancione)

Pancion!: Augmentative of 'pancia' ('Pancion' for 'pancione'), directly assailing his gigantic belly.
Beon!: Agent noun from 'bere' ('Beon' for 'beone'), mocking his notorious appetite for wine and sack.
Briccon!: Classic Italian insult ('Briccon' for 'briccone'), completing the explosive succession of -on rhymes.

In ginocchion!.meaning: on bended knees / kneeling (apocope of in ginocchioni)

In ginocchion!: Adverbial posture idiom ('in ginocchion'), ordering the humiliated knight to prostrate himself like a penitent.
Pancia ritronfia!: Ford's insult pairs 'pancia' with 'ritronfia' (intensive of tronfio, bloated/puffed with self-importance).
Guancia rigonfia!: Alice's matching rhyming retort ('ritronfia / rigonfia'), mocking Falstaff's bloated, pendulous cheeks.
Sconquassaletti!: Inventive Italian compound noun (imperative verb stem 'sconquassa' + plural noun 'letti'), mocking the destructive impact of his weight in bed.
Spaccafarsetti!: Mrs. Quickly's compound noun ('spaccare' + 'farsetti'), deriding the corpulence that splits doublets at the seams.
Vuotabarili!: Pistola's compound noun ('vuotare' + 'barili'), scorning Falstaff's bottomless capacity to drain wine barrels.
Sfiancagiumenti!: Dr. Caius contributes a compound noun ('sfiancare', to exhaust/break the flanks + 'giumenti', packhorses/mares), evoking the poor horses crushed beneath Sir John.
Triplice mento!: Ford's anatomical jab highlighting Falstaff's folds of flesh, rhyming in -ento with the surrounding lines.

Di' che ti penti!.meaning: say / tell (2nd sing. imperative, apocope of dici)

Di' che ti penti!: The chorus demands a formal confession with imperative 'Di'' and subordinate reflexive clause 'che ti penti'.
Ahi! Ahi! mi pento!: Falstaff eagerly repeats 'mi pento' between yelps of pain, desperate to stop the pinching.
Uom frodolento!: Moral denunciation using the archaic Tuscan form 'frodolento' to fit the strict rhyme scheme in -ento.
GLI UOMINI: Libretto character heading marking the male chorus continuing their rhythmic catechism.
Uom turbolento!: Parallel noun phrase castigating Falstaff as a riotous disturber of public and domestic tranquility.

Capron!.meaning: he-goat / billy-goat / lustful old goat (apocope of caprone)

Capron!: Insult mocking both his antlered costume and his lascivious lechery ('Capron' for 'caprone', the quintessential symbol of lust).
Scroccon!: Noun derived from 'scroccare' ('Scroccon' for 'scroccone'), stigmatizing his habit of living at others' expense.
Spaccon!: Insult derived from 'spaccare' ('Spaccon' for 'spaccone'), targeting his bluster and tall tales.
Perdon!: Falstaff's breathless one-word cry for mercy, cleverly rhyming with the barrage of -on insults ('Perdon' for 'perdono').
Riforma la tua vita!: Bardolfo sanctimoniously preaches moral reform to his master, adopting the posture of a holy inquisitor.

Tu puti d'acquavita..meaning: you stink / reek (2nd sing. present of literary putire)

Falstaff unmasks Bardolfo by his breath alone. The verb 'putire' (to stink) governs the preposition 'di' ('d'acquavita'), rhyming hilariously with 'vita'.
LE DONNE: Choral heading for the women taking up the mock-liturgical litany over Falstaff.

Domine fallo casto!.meaning: make him (imperative fa + direct object clitic lo with syntactic doubling)

Domine fallo casto!: Mock-Latin ecclesiastical prayer: Latin vocative 'Domine' combined with Italian causative imperative 'fallo' (fa + lo, with raddoppiamento sintattico).

Ma salvagli l'addomine..meaning: save for him (imperative salva + indirect object clitic gli)
abdomen / belly (comic mock-Latinate form rhyming with Domine)

Boito's celebrated comedic invention: creating a pseudo-Latinized noun 'addomine' (from addome, abdomen/belly) to rhyme with liturgical 'Domine'.
Domine fallo guasto!: Continuation of the mock litany with causative 'fallo guasto' (make him ruined/wretched), rhyming with 'casto'.
Fallo punito domine!: Inverted litany with 'domine' at the cadence, praying for righteous punishment upon the sinner.
Fallo pentito domine!: Couplet completion with 'punito / pentito', pleading for Sir John's complete spiritual repentance.
Formal inquisitorial catechism: addressing Falstaff's spherical shape as a concentrated 'Globo d'impurità', demanding an admission of guilt.

Ben mi sta..meaning: it serves me right / I deserve it (idiomatic expression of resignation)

Colloquial Italian idiom of resignation ('Ben mi sta!'). Falstaff humbly admits his deserved punishment.
Second catechism challenge: 'Monte d'obesità' translates Shakespeare's 'this mountain of mummy' into Boito's grand mock-heroic verse.
Third catechism question: 'Otre di malvasia' evokes Prince Hal's insults of Falstaff as a vessel of wine and sweet Malmsey.

Così sia..meaning: so be it / amen (liturgical closing formula)

Liturgical closing formula 'Così sia' (the standard vernacular rendering of Latin 'Amen'), rhyming with 'malvasia' and concluding the mock-exorcism.
Re dei panciuti!: Bardolfo taunts the pinned-down Falstaff, mocking his immense girth as king of the pot-bellied.

Va' via, tu puti..meaning: go (2nd sing. imperative with apocope apostrophe)

Falstaff recoils from the tormentor leaning over him, complaining of a foul smell. 'Va'' is the truncated imperative of 'andare'; 'puti' is the second-person singular present of 'putire' (to stink).
Re dei cornuti!: Bardolfo continues taunting Falstaff with the traditional insult of the horned cuckold, echoing the stag disguise Falstaff was forced to wear.
Furfanteria!: The chorus shouts epithets denouncing Falstaff's knavery and deceitful tricks.

Ahi! Così sia..meaning: let it be / may it be (3rd sing. present subjunctive)

Falstaff groans in pain and resignation ('Così sia' - Amen / So be it) as the spirits torment him.
Gagliofferia!: The chorus continues its rhythmic insults, accusing Falstaff of clumsy and insolent villainy ('gagliofferia', from 'gaglioffo').
Ed or che il diavol ti porti via!: And now may the devil carry you away!

Ed or che il diavol ti porti via!.meaning: carry away / take away (3rd sing. present subjunctive)

Ed or che il diavol ti porti via!: Bardolfo leans in close over Falstaff to deliver this curse, using the optative subjunctive 'porti via'. His close proximity allows Falstaff to smell his breath and see his unmistakable nose.
Atto terzo Falstaff: Score and libretto structural header marking Act III of Falstaff, appearing here at the transition to Falstaff's unmasking of Bardolfo.
Nitro! Catrame e solfo!: Falstaff immediately detects the chemical, brimstone-like stench of Bardolfo's alcoholic breath, listing the volatile ingredients of gunpowder and brimstone.
Riconosco Bardolfo!: The turning point of the scene: smelling the foul breath and catching sight of the famous red nose beneath the mask, Falstaff realizes his tormentor is merely his own rogue servant in disguise.
Naso vermiglio!: Falstaff begins his torrent of Shakespearean invective directed at Bardolfo's legendary red nose, celebrated throughout Henry IV.
Nasobargiglio!: A vivid Boito compound neologism combining 'naso' (nose) and 'bargiglio' (the fleshy caruncle or wattle of a rooster or turkey), mocking the bumpy, bulbous shape of Bardolfo's nose.
Puntuta lesina!: Metaphor comparing Bardolfo's sharp, piercing nose to a cobbler's awl ('lesina'), which is also proverbial in Italian for stinginess or narrowness.
Vampa di resina!: Falstaff compares the fiery glow of Bardolfo's alcohol-inflamed complexion to resin bursting into flames.
Salamandra! Ignis fatuus! Vecchia alabar: Salamander! Ignis fatuus! Old halberd! Stay

Salamandra! Ignis fatuus! Vecchia alabar.meaning: stay / slat / bone (corset stay or ruler)

Salamandra! Ignis fatuus! Vecchia alabar: A barrage of bizarre metaphors: the mythical fire-dwelling salamander, the Latin 'ignis fatuus' (will-o'-the-wisp / marsh-fire, straight from Shakespeare's 1 Henry IV), an old rusty halberd, and a corset stay/measuring slat ('stecca').
di sartore! Schidion d'inferno! Aringa s: of a tailor! Hell's spit! Dried herring!

Falstaff completes the insult 'stecca di sartore' (a tailor's bone/flat rule) and adds 'schidion d'inferno' (a spit of hell) and 'aringa secca' (dried/pickled herring), echoing Shakespeare's insults for thin, dried-up knaves.

Vampiro! Basilisco!.meaning: basilisk (legendary serpent whose gaze is lethal)

Vampiro! Basilisco!: Falstaff denounces Bardolfo as a monstrous parasite (vampire) and a deadly mythical reptile (basilisk).
Manigoldo! Ladrone!: Direct insults reminding Bardolfo of his true profession as a common thief and ruffian.
Ho detto. E se mentisco: I have spoken. And if I lie

Ho detto. E se mentisco.meaning: I have spoken / I rest my case (passato prossimo 1st sing.)

Ho detto. E se mentisco: 'Ho detto' is a solemn formula ('dixi' / 'I have spoken'). Falstaff sets up a comical oath in the conditional clause 'se mentisco' (if I am lying).
voglio che mi si spacchi il cinturone!: I want my belt to split open!

voglio che mi si spacchi il cinturone!.meaning: burst / split open (3rd sing. present subjunctive)
large belt / sword belt (augmentative of cintura)

voglio che mi si spacchi il cinturone!: Falstaff swears an oath suited to his vast girth: 'may my belt burst!' ('che mi si spacchi il cinturone', with reflexive/mediopassive subjunctive 'si spacchi' and ethical dative 'mi').
Bravo!: The crowd and conspirators applaud Falstaff's brilliant recognition of Bardolfo despite the disguise.
A little pause. I am tired.
Falstaff collapses, catching his breath after the mock exorcism and beating, pleading for a moment of respite.
Come, I will cover you with the white veil.
Mrs. Quickly whispers to Bardolfo, leading him away to be veiled as the 'Queen of the Fairies' for the sham wedding arranged to dupe Dr. Caius.
Ed or, mentre vi passa la scalmana,: And now, while your heat passes off,

Ed or, mentre vi passa la scalmana,.meaning: to you (formal 2nd pers. indirect object clitic)

Ed or, mentre vi passa la scalmana,: Ford steps forward to gloat over the exhausted knight. 'Scalmana' refers to feverish heat or agitation caused by violent exertion.
sir John, dite: il cornuto chi è?: sir John, say: who is the cuckold?
Ford throws Falstaff's earlier boasting in Act II back in his face, asking who turned out to be the real horned victim.
Chi è?: Alice and Meg chime in gleefully to join the mocking interrogation of Falstaff.

Vi siete fatto muto?.meaning: have you become / made yourself (passato prossimo 2nd pers. formal/plur.)

Vi siete fatto muto?: Alice teases Falstaff about his sudden loss of his usual eloquent bluster. 'Farsi' + adjective expresses becoming or turning into.
You are mistaken in the greeting.

Sbagliate nel saluto..meaning: you are mistaken / you err (2nd pers. formal/plur. present)

Alice corrects Falstaff, preparing the grand revelation of her husband's true identity.
Alice unmasks Ford's double identity. The demonstrative pronoun 'questi' is used substantively in literary Italian for a male person near the speaker.
Cavaliero,: Mrs. Quickly addresses Falstaff with mock-solemn courtesy before unleashing a barrage of insults.
voi credeste due donne così grulle,: you believed two women so silly,
Quickly uses the Tuscan adjective 'grullo' (foolish, gullible), questioning Falstaff's absurd conceit.
così citrulle,: Continuation of Quickly's speech: 'citrullo' is a classic Italian term of comical disparagement for a simpleton or blockhead.
da darsi anima e corpo all'avversiero,: as to give themselves body and soul to the adversary,

da darsi anima e corpo all'avversiero,.meaning: to give oneself / surrender oneself (reflexive infinitive)
to the adversary / devil (archaic Italian for the Devil)

da darsi anima e corpo all'avversiero,: Consecutive clause ('da' + infinitive). 'L'avversiero' is an archaic Italian literary designation for Satan/the Devil ('the adversary').
for a man old, filthy, and obese...
Quickly ruthlessly enumerates Falstaff's physical flaws with three devastating adjectives.
Meg and Quickly tag-team to pile on physical mockery, pointing out Falstaff's bald pate.
E con quel peso!: The women unite in a final punchline about Falstaff's staggering weight.
Ford relishes the women's bluntness, noting that their rejection of Falstaff could not be clearer.

Incomincio ad accorgermi.meaning: to realize / notice (reflexive infinitive with 1st sing. clitic mi)

Incomincio ad accorgermi: Falstaff begins to admit his humiliation: 'accorgersi' (to notice/realize) takes 'di' + infinitive.
that I have been a donkey.
Falstaff confesses his foolishness, comparing himself to a donkey ('somaro').
Alice quips that besides an ass, he was also a stag ('cervo'), referring to the antlers of Herne the Hunter he wore.
Ford escalates the animal metaphors, calling him an ox ('bue'), traditionally an emblem of horned cuckolds and dumb, heavy beasts.
E un mostro raro!: Ford caps the animal insults, mocking Falstaff as a freak of nature ('mostro raro'), worthy of being exhibited at a fair.
Ogni sorta di gente dozzinale: Falstaff rallies his dignity, countering the crowd's mockery by labeling them 'gente dozzinale' (cheap, dime-a-dozen mediocre people).
mi beffa e se ne gloria;: mocks me and boasts of it;

mi beffa e se ne gloria;.meaning: boasts of it / prides itself on it (reflexive verb with partitive/pronominal ne)

mi beffa e se ne gloria;: Falstaff observes that mediocre minds find glory only in mocking their betters. Note the pronominal construction 'se ne gloria' (glories in it).
pur, senza me, costor con tanta boria: yet, without me, these people with so much arrogance

pur, senza me, costor con tanta boria.meaning: these people (pejorative demonstrative pronoun, apocope of costoro)

pur, senza me, costor con tanta boria: Falstaff begins his Shakespearean vindication: 'costoro' (truncated to 'costor') carries a disdainful nuance for those displaying unearned arrogance ('boria').
would not have a pinch of salt.
'Sale' (salt) is proverbial in Italian and Latin ('sales') for wit and intelligence ('sale in zucca'). Without Falstaff, these simple townsfolk would have no wit at all.
It is I who make you shrewd.

Son io che vi fa scaltri..meaning: I am (1st sing. present, apocope of sono)
makes (3rd sing. present agreeing with relative pronoun che)

Boito's magnificent Italian translation of Shakespeare's famous line ('I am not only witty in myself, but the cause that wit is in other men'). Falstaff asserts intellectual superiority over his persecutors.
L'arguzia mia crea l'arguzia degli altri: My wit creates the wit of the others.
The crowning philosophical declaration of Falstaff's character: his boundless wit inspires and animates the humor of everyone around him.
Ma bravo!: The crowd and conspirators are forced to admire Falstaff's irrepressible wit and audacity.
FORD Per gli dèi!: Ford swears by the gods in exasperated admiration of Falstaff's sheer nerve.
Se non ridessi ti sconquasserei!: If I weren't laughing I would smash you to pieces!

Se non ridessi ti sconquasserei!.meaning: I laughed / were laughing (1st sing. imperfect subjunctive)
I would smash / shatter / batter (1st sing. conditional)

Se non ridessi ti sconquasserei!: Hypothetical period of unreality: imperfect subjunctive ('ridessi') + present conditional ('sconquasserei'). Ford admits that Falstaff's humor disarms his wrath.
But enough. And now I want you to listen to me.

Ma basta. Ed ora vo' che m'ascoltiate..meaning: it is enough / that will do (3rd sing. present)
I want (apocope of voglio with apostrophe)
you listen to (2nd pers. plur. present subjunctive)

Ford calls for order to stage his own planned trick. 'Vo'' is the apocopated form of 'voglio', taking a subjunctive clause ('che m'ascoltiate').
Coronerem la mascherata bella: We shall crown the lovely masquerade

Coronerem la mascherata bella.meaning: we shall crown (1st pers. plur. future, apocope of coroneremo)

Coronerem la mascherata bella: Ford announces the culmination of the night's revels: the wedding ceremony he believes will marry Dr. Caius to Nannetta.
co' gli sponsali della: 'Co'' is an archaic contraction of 'con'. 'Sponsali' (espousals/wedding) belongs to elevated, formal legal and poetic diction.
Nannetta was disguised as the Fairy Queen in Act III; Ford believes she is the bride being led forward.

Già s'avanza la coppia degli sposi..meaning: advances / steps forward (3rd sing. present reflexive)

Ford points out the approaching masked pair (unaware that Quickly has substituted Bardolfo under the fairy veil).

Attenti!.meaning: attentive / careful (used as plural imperative interjection)

Attenti!: Ford commands silence and vigilance from the assembled throng.
Eccola, in bianca vesta: Here she is, in white garment

Eccola, in bianca vesta.meaning: here she is (presentative ecco + feminine clitic la)
garment / dress / robe (poetic form of veste)

Eccola, in bianca vesta: Ford recognizes the pre-arranged white dress of the Fairy Queen, unaware that Bardolfo is disguised within it.
col velo e il serto delle rose in testa: with the veil and the garland of roses on her head
Ford details the precise costume tokens he had instructed Caius to look for, which the merry wives have cleverly shifted onto Bardolfo.
and her betrothed whom I arranged for her.
Ford gloats over his paternal authority in arranging Dr. Caius as Nannetta's groom ('ch'io le disposi').

Circondatela, o ninfe..meaning: surround her (2nd pers. plur. imperative + clitic la)

Ford directs the masquerading nymphs and spirits to encircle the bridal couple.
Un'altra coppia: Alice steps forward with the second disguised couple (Fenton and Nannetta), setting up the counter-trap for Ford.

d'amanti desïosi.meaning: longing / eager / desirous (with poetic dieresis desïosi)

d'amanti desïosi: Alice describes Fenton and Nannetta poetically with the archaic/lyric form 'desïosi' (four syllables, marked by dieresis).
chiede d'essere ammessa agli augurosi: asks to be admitted to the auspicious
Alice uses formal, ceremonial diction ('augurosi connubi') to coax Ford into blessing both marriages simultaneously.
connubi!: 'Connubio' (plural 'connubi') is elevated Latinate poetic diction for marriage.
So be it. We shall make the feast a double one.

E sia. Farem la festa doppia..meaning: so be it / let it be (subjunctive idiom)
we shall make (future 1st pers. plur., apocope of faremo)

In his smug confidence, Ford eagerly agrees to double the wedding celebration, unwittingly walking directly into Alice's trap.

Avvicinate i lumi..meaning: bring closer / near (2nd pers. plur. imperative)

Ford orders the torches and lanterns brought close to illuminate the climax of the ceremony.
Ford pronounces the binding paternal blessing: 'Heaven unites you', legally sealing both marriages.
Giù le maschere e i veli. Apoteosi!: Down with the masks and veils. Apotheosis!
Ford theatrically calls for the grand revelation ('Apoteosi!'), expecting Caius and Nannetta to emerge.
Ah! Ah! Ah! Ah!: Wild, uncontrollable laughter sweeps through the assembly as the unmasked couples are revealed.
Spavento!: Dr. Caius recoils in horror upon seeing that his 'bride' beneath the veil is the drunken, red-nosed Bardolfo.
Tradimento!: Ford gasps in dismay as he realizes he has been completely outwitted and duped into marrying his daughter to Fenton.

GLI ALTRI.meaning: the others (chorus / rest of the company)

GLI ALTRI: Score and libretto rubric indicating the chorus ('THE OTHERS') shouting in response.
Apoteosi!: The crowd mockingly throws Ford's own triumphant word ('Apoteosi!') back at him.
Fenton con mia figlia!: Ford realizes to his dismay that the second couple he just solemnly blessed was none other than Fenton and Nannetta.
Ho sposato Bardolfo!: Dr. Caius shrieks in disbelief at his horrifying discovery: instead of young Nannetta, he has wed Falstaff's scoundrel follower Bardolfo.
Vittoria!: Alice and the women celebrate their complete victory over both Ford's rigid patriarchal scheme and Dr. Caius's unwanted suit.
Evviva! Evviva!: The entire company cheers the young lovers' triumph and the hilarious poetic justice.
Oh! Meraviglia!: Ford stands dumbfounded, marveling at the audacity and perfection of Alice's scheme.
L'uom cade spesso nelle reti ordite: Man often falls into the nets woven

L'uom cade spesso nelle reti ordite.meaning: woven / plotted / devised (past participle fem. plur.)

L'uom cade spesso nelle reti ordite: Alice delivers a moral axiom: people who plot deceptions often become trapped in snares of their own making.
Prepositional agent phrase dependent on 'ordite'. 'Malizia' here denotes sly plots and scheming calculations.
Caro buon messer Ford, ed ora, dite:: Dear good Master Ford, and now, tell:
Falstaff seizes his moment of sweetest revenge, mimicking Ford's exact gloating tone from earlier in the scene.

lo scornato chi è?.meaning: hoodwinked / mocked / deflated / disgraced (used as substantive noun)

lo scornato chi è?: Falstaff mirrors Ford's question 'il cornuto chi è?' (who is the cuckold?), substituting 'scornato' (shamed/duped) to turn the tables completely on Ford.

Lui..meaning: he / him (3rd sing. masculine tonic pronoun)

Ford desperately deflects the blame and ridicule onto Dr. Caius.

Voi..meaning: you (2nd pers. plural / formal tonic pronoun)

Bardolfo chimes in cheekily from under his bridal veil, addressing Ford and Caius.
Fenton gloats at the pair of disappointed intriguers, using the truncated tonic pronoun 'lor'.

Noi..meaning: we / us (1st pers. plural tonic pronoun)

Caius finally concedes that both he and Ford have been thoroughly hoodwinked together.
Falstaff gloats triumphantly: not just one, but both Ford and Caius are the dupes.
Alice delivers the definitive verdict: Falstaff, Ford, and Caius have all three been outwitted by the women.
Turn around and behold those graceful anxieties.

Volgiti e mira quelle ansie leggiadre..meaning: turn around (2nd sing. imperative + reflexive clitic ti)

Alice appeals to Ford's paternal heart, directing his gaze toward his trembling daughter and her true love Fenton.

Perdonateci, padre..meaning: forgive us (2nd pers. plur./formal imperative + clitic ci)

Nannetta kneels before Ford, pleading for his fatherly forgiveness and blessing for her marriage to Fenton.
Chi schivare non può la propria noia: Whoever cannot avoid his own misfortune
Ford accepts defeat with philosophical grace: 'noia' here retains its archaic and literary sense of harm, grief, or vexation.
let him accept it with good grace.

l'accetti di buon grado..meaning: let him accept / may he accept (3rd sing. present subjunctive)

Jussive/concessive subjunctive ('l'accetti') governing the idiomatic prepositional phrase 'di buon grado' (readily, graciously).
Facciamo il parentado: Let us make the family alliance

Facciamo il parentado.meaning: let us make (1st pers. plur. imperative/subjunctive)

Facciamo il parentado: Ford blesses the union: 'fare il parentado' is a classic Italian expression for sealing a kinship tie through marriage.
and may heaven give you joy.
Optative subjunctive ('che il ciel vi dia gioia'), conferring Ford's heartfelt paternal blessing upon Fenton and Nannetta.
A chorus and let us end the scene.

Un coro e terminiam la scena..meaning: let us end / finish (1st pers. plur. imperative, apocope of terminiamo)

Falstaff breaks the fourth wall with theatrical metadrama, proposing to conclude the opera with a grand ensemble choral fugue.
E poi con sir Falstaff, tutti, andiamo a: And then with Sir Falstaff, all of us, let us go to dinner.

E poi con sir Falstaff, tutti, andiamo a.meaning: let us go (1st pers. plur. imperative)

E poi con sir Falstaff, tutti, andiamo a: Ford graciously invites Falstaff and the entire town to feast together at his house, ending all rivalry in conviviality.
Everything in the world is a joke.
The opening subject of Verdi's supreme comic masterpiece fugue: Boito's summation of human comedy, declaring that all worldly vanities are but a jest.
L'uom è nato burlone,: Continuation of the fugue subject: human nature is inherently foolish and jesting ('burlone').
la fede in cor gli ciurla,: 'Ciurlare nel manico' is a Tuscan idiom meaning to waver or prove unsteady; here 'gli ciurla' describes how conviction and certainty totter within man's heart.
Parallel inversion with line 105: human reason reels and stumbles, helpless in the face of life's chaotic absurdities.

Tutti gabbati! Irride.meaning: mocks / laughs at / derides (3rd sing. present)

Tutti gabbati! Irride: 'Tutti gabbati!' (Everyone is fooled/hoodwinked!) is the universal verdict of the opera. Enjambment carries the verb 'irride' over to the next line.
Synthesizes the universal condition of mankind: every mortal mocks his neighbor, unaware that he too is equally foolish.
Ma ride ben chi ride: But he laughs well who laughs
Italian proverb: 'Ride bene chi ride l'ultimo' (He who laughs last laughs best), adapted by Boito into poetic octosyllable.
The final line of Giuseppe Verdi's operatic career: the ultimate triumph of laughter, wisdom, and compassionate comedy over tragedy.
